docs.title: Inertial Navigation Simulation & GUI
docs.text:
ins_sim is an open-source 6-DOF, WGS-84 strapdown INS Monte Carlo simulator with a desktop GUI. It generates a truth flight trajectory, derives the gyro and accelerometer outputs a perfect IMU would produce along it, corrupts them with the errors of a real IMU, and runs a strapdown mechanization to recover position, velocity, and attitude. A Monte Carlo ensemble over independent draws of the sensor errors shows how navigation error grows over time for a given IMU.

Download the app View on GitHub

docs.title: Core features
docs.text:
• Truth trajectories from YAML missions: take-off, climbs and descents, waypoint legs, holding patterns and speed changes, written in aviation units and converted to SI.
  • An IMU error model from the datasheet: angle and velocity random walk, turn-on and in-run biases with the bias instability entered as the datasheet gives it, scale-factor and misalignment errors, and initial alignment errors.
  • Rotating-Earth strapdown mechanization: Earth rate, transport rate, WGS-84 radii of curvature and normal gravity, evaluated at the current position every step, not a flat-Earth approximation. An optional precision update, with coning and sculling corrections, can be tested against the outputs of an integrating IMU.
  • Vertical channel physics: a third-order baro-damped loop by default, aided by a barometer with its own errors (temperature, altimeter setting, weather, noise), or free-inertial to watch the channel's instability.
  • Monte Carlo evaluation: independent error draws for every trial, errors measured as the textbook defines them, and CEP, ±3σ and percentile statistics.
  • Covariance analysis and error budget: the same statistics predicted in one pass by a 43-state linearized error model, and each error source's share of them.
  • Interactive visualizations: every tab is a plotly page rendered in the app: CEP growth with an hourly table, attitude, velocity and position errors with ±3σ bands, a 3D trajectory with its 95th-percentile error tube, and a ground-track map.
  • Checked against the textbook: the Schuler oscillation, the bias responses, the vertical channel and the noise statistics all match their analytic predictions on the Validation page.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Data flows from truth generation, through the IMU error model, into the strapdown navigator, and is summarized by the Monte Carlo evaluation:

flowchart TD
    CFG["Config (YAML)<br/>mission + IMU spec"]
    TRUTH["Truth generation<br/>trajectory/kinematics.py"]
    SENSOR["IMU error model<br/>sensors/imu.py"]
    NAV["Strapdown mechanization<br/>navigation/strapdown.py"]
    EVAL["Monte Carlo + plots<br/>evaluation/"]
    EARTH(["Earth model<br/>core/earth_model.py"])

    CFG --> TRUTH
    TRUTH -->|"ideal ω_ib^b, f_ib^b"| SENSOR
    SENSOR -->|"measured ω_ib^b, f_ib^b"| NAV
    NAV -->|"position, velocity, attitude"| EVAL
    EARTH -.->|"ω_ie, ω_en, g, R_N/R_E"| TRUTH
    EARTH -.-> NAV

docs.title: Conventions in brief
docs.text:
• Notation: the symbols of Groves (2013), in these pages and in the Python names. v_eb_n is \(\vvec{eb}{n}\), the velocity of the body (b) relative to the Earth (e), resolved along North-East-Down axes (n). Notation & conventions defines every symbol.
  • Frames: the North-East-Down navigation frame (n) at the current position, and the body frame (b): x forward, y right, z down.
  • Attitude: the body-to-NED transformation \(\Cmat{b}{n}\), held as a scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation. Quaternions are scalar-last, [x, y, z, w].
  • Radii of curvature: \(R_N\) is the meridian radius and \(R_E\) the transverse one. Many texts use \(R_N\) for the transverse radius.
  • Errors: always the estimate minus the truth.
  • Units: SI inside the simulator. The YAML files and the app use datasheet and aviation units (degrees, feet, knots, °/h, µg), converted when read; see Units & constants.

docs.title: Download & Install
docs.text:
Prebuilt portable bundles for Windows and Linux (x86-64 and ARM64) are attached to every GitHub Release. No Python installation is required — download, extract, and run.

Download for Windows Download for Linux

On the release page, grab the asset for your platform:

Platform Asset Run Windows (64-bit) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-windows-x86_64.zip extract, run ins_sim.exe Linux (x86-64) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-x86_64.tar.gz extract, run ins_sim Linux (ARM64) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz extract, run ins_sim

Which Linux asset?

Run uname -m on the target machine: x86_64 → use the x86-64 asset; aarch64 → use the ARM64 asset. The ARM64 bundle covers Raspberry Pi 4/5 running the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS and other ARM64/aarch64 Linux. 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS (armv7l) is not covered by a prebuilt bundle — see Raspberry Pi (32-bit) below.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Download the .zip asset and extract it anywhere (no installer).
  2. Open the extracted ins_sim folder and run ins_sim.exe.

Windows SmartScreen

The binaries are not code-signed, so the first launch may show "Windows protected your PC". Click More info → Run anyway. Keep ins_sim.exe inside its folder — it needs the bundled libraries beside it.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Pick the asset matching your CPU (uname -m) — x86_64 or aarch64:

# Intel/AMD 64-bit
tar xzf ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./ins_sim/ins_sim

# ARM64 (aarch64)
tar xzf ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz
./ins_sim/ins_sim

Runtime requirements

Bundles are built on Ubuntu 24.04, so a similarly recent glibc is required. Like other desktop apps, ins_sim uses your system's own libraries for graphics, fonts, sound and encryption, which a desktop installation already has. If the app stops with error while loading shared libraries, or the result tabs say a library failed to load, install the package that provides the library it names. Minimal installations, the ARM64 bundle and X11 sessions usually need these:

sudo apt-get install libegl1 libgl1 libxkbcommon0 libnss3 libasound2t64 libopus0 libminizip1t64 libsnappy1v5 libxcb-cursor0

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
The ARM64 bundle (ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz) is the one for a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 — but only when it is running the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. Confirm first:

uname -m        # aarch64  → use the ARM64 bundle
                # armv7l   → 32-bit OS, see below

docs.title: Raspberry Pi (32-bit)
docs.text:
There is no prebuilt bundle for 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS (armv7l/armhf), and the desktop GUI cannot be installed there either — PySide6 publishes no 32-bit ARM wheels, so pip install ".[gui]" will not resolve. Two options, best first:

  1. Reflash to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS (the Pi 4/5 support it) and use the aarch64 bundle above, or run the GUI from source.

  2. Stay on 32-bit and run the headless CLI from source — it needs only numpy/scipy/pyyaml/matplotlib/plotly, no Qt:

    git clone https://github.com/jorgieo/ins_sim.git
cd ins_sim
pip install -e .          # base install, NOT ".[gui]"
python main.py            # writes an interactive maps/trajectory_map.html

    This produces the matplotlib summary figure and a standalone interactive ground-track map (open maps/trajectory_map.html in a browser) without the desktop front end. See the CLI options with python main.py --help.

docs.title: Internet access
docs.text: The application runs fully offline with one exception: the Map tab loads OpenStreetMap basemap tiles from the network. Every other visualization works without a connection.

docs.title: Run from source
docs.text:
Prefer a Python environment? Clone the repository and launch the GUI directly:

git clone https://github.com/jorgieo/ins_sim.git
cd ins_sim
pip install ".[gui]"
python -m ins_sim.gui

docs.title: Your first simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial runs the packaged mission in the desktop app, reads the main results, and then shows the one thing an inertial navigator cannot do on its own. It takes about ten minutes and needs no programming.

You need the app installed: see Download & install. The map in step 6 also needs an internet connection, for its background tiles.

docs.title: 1. Open the app
docs.text:
Start the app: ins_sim.exe on Windows, ./ins_sim/ins_sim on Linux, or python -m ins_sim.gui if you run it from a source checkout.

The window has two parts. The control panel on the left holds every setting. The results area on the right says Run a simulation to see results until you do.

The first time it starts, the app creates two folders next to itself, trajectories and imu_specs, and puts a copy of the packaged mission and IMU spec in them. These are the files the two lists at the top of the control panel show.

docs.title: 2. Look at the mission and the IMU
docs.text:
Two files describe a simulation:

  • The mission (Trajectory list): bqn_departure.yaml. An 80-minute flight from Rafael Hernández Airport (BQN) at the north-west corner of Puerto Rico. The aircraft takes off, climbs to 15,000 ft and flies five circles in a holding pattern off the north coast. It then crosses the island to hold again south of it, and finally accelerates to Mach 0.8 for a sprint to the south-west: 440 nautical miles in all.
  • The IMU (IMU spec list): imu_spec.yaml. A navigation-grade unit, of the ring-laser-gyro kind that airliners carry. Its gyro biases drift by about 0.01 °/h.

Leave both as they are.

docs.title: 3. Choose quick settings
docs.text:
The defaults, 50 trials at a 0.1 s time step, give the most precise results but take about ten minutes. For a first look, set:

  • Monte Carlo iterations: 10 trials. Each trial flies the same mission with a fresh draw of every sensor error, so ten trials show ten possible outcomes.
  • Time step (dt): 1.00 s. The navigator updates once per second instead of ten times.

Leave Baro altitude aiding checked, and every box under Output Visualizations checked: each one becomes a tab of results.

docs.title: 4. Run
docs.text: Click Run Simulation. The log under the button reports each step, and the progress bar fills as the trials complete. After about 15 seconds the results appear:

docs.title: 5. Read the CEP tab
docs.text:
The first tab shows how far each trial's position estimate is from the truth, horizontally, in nautical miles, over the flight's 1.3 hours. Every faint line is one trial.

  • The trials spread out because each one drew different sensor errors. Ten trials of the same IMU end anywhere from 0.3 to 3.7 nmi off.
  • The CEP, the circular error probable, is the radius that holds half of the trials. The table under the plot gives it at each whole hour: 0.90 nmi after one hour, while 95% of the trials are within 2.44 nmi.
  • The dashed orange line is a straight-line fit to the CEP over the first hour. Its slope, here 0.97 nmi per hour, is the usual one-number summary of an INS: this IMU makes a "one nautical mile per hour" navigator, as expected of navigation grade.
  • The dashed crimson line, and the table's last row, is the CEP that a covariance analysis predicts without random trials: 1.17 nmi after one hour. Ten trials are few, so their CEP of 0.90 nmi differs from it; with more trials the two come together. The Error Budget tab shows which error source contributes most.

The app always uses the same random seed, so the same settings give the same numbers every time.

docs.title: 6. Look at the position errors and the map
docs.text:
Open the Position Errors tab. It shows the North, East and Down errors over time: a dark line for the average over the trials, and a shaded band of ±3 standard deviations around it. The North and East bands keep widening, to kilometres, but the Down band levels off at a few hundred metres once the climb ends. The barometric altimeter holds the height, to within its own errors, as the next step shows.

Then open the Map tab: the true track over Puerto Rico, every trial's estimated track, and a shaded band that holds 95% of the trials. White dots mark every five minutes. The band widens along the flight as the errors grow. Hover over the track to read the time and the error.

docs.title: 7. Switch off the barometer
docs.text:
An inertial navigator measures height by integrating acceleration, and that calculation is unstable. Gravity weakens with height, so a navigator that thinks it is too high computes too little gravity. It then believes it is accelerating upward, which makes its height error grow further. Aircraft use a barometric altimeter to hold this in check, and so does the simulator, unless you switch it off.

Uncheck Baro altitude aiding, click Run Simulation again and open Position Errors:

The Down error now grows roughly tenfold every 20 minutes: about 600 m (3σ) after 10 minutes, 35 km after 40 minutes and 2,000 km by the end. The axis labels use SI prefixes: 50k is 50 km and 2M is 2,000 km. The height error also corrupts the horizontal solution: the CEP after one hour is now 2.5 nmi instead of 0.9. The Vertical channel page explains the instability and the loop that tames it.

Check the box again before your next run.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Reading the results explains every tab.
  • Modelling an IMU has tactical-grade and MEMS specs to try, and shows how to enter your own sensor's datasheet.
  • Writing a mission shows how to fly your own route.
  • Your first script runs the same simulation from Python.
  • The INS error model explains why the errors grow the way they do.

docs.title: Your first script
docs.text: The desktop app is a thin layer over a Python package, and everything it does you can do from a script. This tutorial repeats Your first simulation in about 30 lines of Python: build the truth, load the IMU spec, run the Monte Carlo trials, measure the position error and plot it. You get the same numbers as the app.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
You need Python 3.11 or later. Get the source and install it:

git clone https://github.com/jorgieo/ins_sim.git
cd ins_sim
pip install -e .

The -e keeps the installation linked to the folder, so a later git pull updates it. Scripts do not need the desktop app's gui extra.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
Save this as first_script.py anywhere and run it with python first_script.py:

"""Your first script: a Monte Carlo run on the packaged mission, step by step."""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_imu_spec_path, default_trajectory_path
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.evaluation.monte_carlo import run_monte_carlo
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import load_imu_spec
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

# 1. The truth: the packaged mission, sampled every second.
truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(default_trajectory_path()), tau_i=1.0)
print(f"Mission: {truth.t[-1] / 60:.1f} min, {len(truth.t)} samples")

# 2. The IMU: the packaged navigation-grade spec, converted to SI units.
spec = load_imu_spec(str(default_imu_spec_path()))
print(f"Gyro bias instability: {np.rad2deg(spec.gyro_bias_instability) * 3600:.3f} deg/h")

# 3. Ten trials, each with its own draw of every sensor error.
mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=10, seed=42)

# 4. Position error, estimate minus truth, in metres along North, East, Down.
delta_r_eb_n = position_error(mc.est_L_b, mc.est_lambda_b, mc.est_h_b,
                              truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)
horizontal = np.hypot(delta_r_eb_n[..., 0], delta_r_eb_n[..., 1])  # (trials, samples)
cep = np.median(horizontal, axis=0)

one_hour = np.searchsorted(truth.t, 3600.0)
print(f"CEP after 1 h: {cep[one_hour] / 1852:.2f} nmi")

# 5. Every trial's horizontal error, and their median, the CEP.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(truth.t / 60, horizontal.T / 1852, color="0.75", linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot(truth.t / 60, cep / 1852, color="#2a78d6", linewidth=2.5, label="CEP")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (min)", ylabel="Horizontal error (nmi)",
       title="Navigation-grade IMU on the packaged mission, 10 trials")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.savefig("first_script.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
print("Saved first_script.png")

It prints:

Mission: 79.8 min, 4791 samples
Gyro bias instability: 0.010 deg/h
CEP after 1 h: 0.90 nmi
Saved first_script.png

and saves the plot shown at the end of this page. The rest of the page goes through it step by step.

docs.title: 1. The truth
docs.text:
# 1. The truth: the packaged mission, sampled every second.
truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(default_trajectory_path()), tau_i=1.0)
print(f"Mission: {truth.t[-1] / 60:.1f} min, {len(truth.t)} samples")

build_trajectory reads the mission file and flies it, phase by phase, sampling the result every tau_i seconds: here once a second, like the app's Time step of 1.00 s. The truth it returns holds, at each of the 4,791 samples, the true position, velocity and attitude, and the outputs a perfect IMU would give along the way. The other two values it returns, ignored here, describe the mission's sprint speed and turn radius.

docs.title: 2. The IMU spec
docs.text:
# 2. The IMU: the packaged navigation-grade spec, converted to SI units.
spec = load_imu_spec(str(default_imu_spec_path()))
print(f"Gyro bias instability: {np.rad2deg(spec.gyro_bias_instability) * 3600:.3f} deg/h")

load_imu_spec reads the YAML file, which is written in datasheet units, and converts every value to SI. The bias instability, entered as 0.01 °/h, is held in rad/s; the script converts it back to check.

docs.title: 3. The Monte Carlo run
docs.text:
# 3. Ten trials, each with its own draw of every sensor error.
mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=10, seed=42)

Each trial draws its own set of sensor errors, corrupts the perfect IMU outputs with them, and runs the strapdown navigator from the true starting point, with a drawn alignment error. The result holds every trial's estimates: mc.est_L_b is the estimated latitude, an array of shape (10, 4791), one row per trial. This step takes about ten seconds.

The seed fixes the random draws, so the run is repeatable. The app uses 42 as well, which is why this script reproduces its results.

docs.title: 4. The position error
docs.text:
# 4. Position error, estimate minus truth, in metres along North, East, Down.
delta_r_eb_n = position_error(mc.est_L_b, mc.est_lambda_b, mc.est_h_b,
                              truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)
horizontal = np.hypot(delta_r_eb_n[..., 0], delta_r_eb_n[..., 1])  # (trials, samples)
cep = np.median(horizontal, axis=0)

one_hour = np.searchsorted(truth.t, 3600.0)
print(f"CEP after 1 h: {cep[one_hour] / 1852:.2f} nmi")

position_error subtracts the truth from each estimate and converts the latitude, longitude and height differences to metres along North, East and Down. The horizontal error is the length of the North and East components, and its median across the trials at each moment is the CEP. After one hour it is 0.90 nmi, the same as in the app's CEP table.

docs.title: 5. The plot
docs.text:
# 5. Every trial's horizontal error, and their median, the CEP.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(truth.t / 60, horizontal.T / 1852, color="0.75", linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot(truth.t / 60, cep / 1852, color="#2a78d6", linewidth=2.5, label="CEP")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (min)", ylabel="Horizontal error (nmi)",
       title="Navigation-grade IMU on the packaged mission, 10 trials")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.savefig("first_script.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
print("Saved first_script.png")

Like the app's CEP tab, the plot shows each trial in grey and their median in blue.

docs.title: Names that look like symbols
docs.text: The variables follow the textbook symbols on the Notation & conventions page: L_b is the latitude \(L_b\), and delta_r_eb_n is the position error \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\). A prefix gives a value's role: est_ for the navigator's estimate, meas_ for a sensor output and delta_ for an error, always the estimate minus the truth.
