docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
This guide explains how to use ins_sim in practice: the desktop app's controls on this page, then one page per task. If you have not run the app yet, start with Your first simulation.

Page Read it to Reading the results understand every results tab Writing a mission fly your own route Modelling an IMU simulate your own sensor, from its datasheet Command-line runs run simulations without the desktop app Recipes answer common questions: which error dominates, how many trials, which time step

docs.title: The window
docs.text: The control panel on the left holds the settings, from top to bottom: the mission, the simulation settings, the result tabs to build, and the Run Simulation button with its progress bar and log. The results area on the right shows one tab per result once a run finishes.

docs.title: Missions and IMU specs
docs.text:
Every simulation needs two YAML files: a mission, chosen in the Trajectory list, and an IMU spec, chosen in the IMU spec list.

The lists show the files in two folders, trajectories and imu_specs, that the app creates next to itself the first time it starts:

How you run the app Where the folders are The downloaded app In the app's own folder, beside ins_sim.exe or ins_sim From source (python -m ins_sim.gui) In the folder you start it from Either, when that folder is read-only In ins_sim in your home folder

Each folder starts with a copy of the packaged file: bqn_departure.yaml and imu_spec.yaml. To add your own, save a new .yaml file in the folder. The list picks it up the next time you open it, without a restart. The app never overwrites your files. To get a packaged file back, delete or rename your copy and restart the app.

A list only shows files that look right: a mission must have a phases section, and an IMU spec must have gyro and accel sections. Browse… adds a file from anywhere else, for the current session.

How to write the files is the subject of Writing a mission and Modelling an IMU.

docs.title: Simulation settings
docs.text:
Monte Carlo iterations (1–1,000, default 50) is the number of trials. Each trial flies the same mission with a fresh draw of every sensor error, and the results are statistics over the trials. More trials give smoother, more trustworthy statistics but take proportionally longer: Recipes suggests how many you need.

Time step (dt) (0.01–10 s, default 0.1 s) is the interval at which the truth is sampled and the navigator updates, \(\tau_i\) on the theory pages. The run time is proportional to the number of steps. As a guide, on a desktop PC each trial of the packaged 80-minute mission takes:

Time step One trial 10 trials 50 trials 1.0 s about 1 s about 15 s about 1 min 0.1 s about 13 s about 2 min about 11 min

A 1 s step is fine for a quick look at how the errors grow. Use 0.1 s for final numbers.

Baro altitude aiding (checked by default) feeds a barometric altimeter's height into the navigator's height channel. The altimeter errs as the IMU spec's baro block says, or reports the true height if the spec has none (see Modelling an IMU). Without aiding the height error grows exponentially: try it in Your first simulation. The Vertical channel page explains why.

Advanced (collapsed by default; click it to open) holds two settings that change how the navigation algorithm itself is tested. Leave them alone to study sensor errors.

  • Truth oversampling (Off, or 2–100 per step). Off, the perfect IMU's outputs are built to match the navigator's basic update exactly, so the only errors are the sensors'. Set to N, the mission is built N times per time step and the IMU reports averages over each step, as a real integrating IMU does. The navigator's own error then shows too. Larger N is more faithful but slower to build: N = 10 at a 0.1 s step adds about 8 s to the run.
  • Mechanization: Basic or Precision. The precision update corrects for the vehicle turning within each step (coning, sculling and rotation corrections) and takes about 1.4 times as long. It belongs with truth oversampling; without it the log prints a note, because the precision corrections then add an error of their own.

With perfect sensors, on the packaged mission at 0.1 s with oversampling at 10, the basic update alone puts the track up to 1.7 km off, and the precision update about 2 m. The Strapdown mechanization page explains the difference.

Output Visualizations selects the result tabs to build. Each tab takes a moment to build when the run finishes, so unchecking the ones you do not need saves a little time. The Error Budget tab, and the dashed predicted lines on the others, come from a covariance analysis that the app runs after the trials; it takes a few seconds.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Run Simulation starts the run in the background, so the window stays responsive. The controls are disabled until it finishes, and the button becomes Cancel: click it, or press Esc, to stop the run after the current trial. If at least two trials finished, the app asks whether to show their results; otherwise, or if you decline, the previous results stay on screen. Closing the window during a run asks whether to stop it first. The log reports the mission's length and duration, each completed trial, and the run time with the final 95th-percentile error. If a file has a mistake, a Simulation failed message names the problem; see Writing a mission for the common ones.

Every run uses the same random seed, 42, so the same files and settings always give the same results. On the same mission and time step, changing the IMU spec changes the results only through that change: see Recipes.

docs.title: Offline use
docs.text: The app needs no network connection, except for the background tiles of the Map tab, which come from OpenStreetMap. Without a connection the map still shows the tracks and the error band, on a blank background.

docs.title: Command-line runs
docs.text: main.py, at the top of the source repository, runs the same simulation as the desktop app without its window. It suits batch runs, and computers where the app cannot be installed. It comes with the source code, not with the downloadable app: install from source first, as in Your first script.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
From the repository folder:

python main.py                      # packaged mission and IMU, 20 trials
python main.py --trials 100 --dt 0.1 --imu-spec my_imu.yaml
Option Default Meaning --config the packaged mission Mission YAML file --imu-spec the packaged navigation-grade spec IMU spec YAML file --trials 20 Number of Monte Carlo trials --dt 0.1 Time step [s] --seed 42 Random seed; the app always uses 42 --mechanization basic Strapdown update, basic or precision --oversample off Build the truth this many times per step, for an integrating IMU

The last two match the app's Advanced settings (see the User guide); use them together. Baro altitude aiding is always on. python main.py --help lists the options.

docs.title: What it prints
docs.text:
With --trials 10 --dt 1.0 it prints:

Total path  : 440.2 nm  (815 km)
Duration    : 79.8 min  (4790 s)
Samples     : 4,791  (dt=1.0 s)
Start g     : 9.78530 m/s²
Zero-noise error  start: 0.000 m  max: 0.0 m  end: 0.0 m
  t = 8.0 min (10%): err = 0.0 m
  t = 19.9 min (25%): err = 0.0 m
  t = 39.9 min (50%): err = 0.0 m
  t = 59.9 min (75%): err = 0.0 m
  t = 79.8 min (100%): err = 0.0 m
Max |dv_eb_n/dt|: 5.65 m/s²
Max |f_ib_b|: 11.36 m/s²
95th-pct error  start:  0.000 m   end: 6688.3 m
Error budget (covariance analysis): CEP with each source alone [NM], and its share of the horizontal variance
                                                    60 min
  Initial alignment                            0.53 ( 27%)
  Gyro biases                                  0.56 ( 20%)
  Gyro scale factor and misalignment           0.71 ( 40%)
  Accelerometer biases                         0.18 (  2%)
  Accel. scale factor and misalignment         0.35 (  8%)
  Sensor noise (ARW and VRW)                   0.20 (  3%)
  Barometer                                    0.00 (  0%)
  All sources: predicted CEP                          1.17
Predicted CEP at the end: 1.51 NM; Monte Carlo: 1.73 NM
Monte Carlo simulation time: 0h 0m 22s
Interactive map saved: .../ins_sim/maps/trajectory_map.html
  • The mission: its length in nautical miles ("nm") and kilometres, its duration, the number of samples, and gravity at the start.
  • The zero-noise check: the navigator, fed the outputs of a perfect IMU, must follow the truth exactly; the error is printed at five points of the flight. It is 0.0 m for any mission, because the perfect outputs are built to match the navigator, so it checks the software rather than your mission; see Validation. With --oversample it is instead the navigator's own integration error.
  • The largest acceleration and specific force along the mission, a check that the flight is physically reasonable. 11.36 m/s² is about 1.16 g, in the holding patterns' 30° turns.
  • The result: the 95th percentile of the 3D position error at the start and the end.
  • The error budget of the covariance analysis: each error source's predicted CEP on its own and its share of the horizontal variance, at each whole hour of flight (or at the end of a shorter one), then the predicted CEP of all sources. The last line compares the predicted CEP at the end with the trials' CEP, which 10 trials pin down only to about 20%.
  • The run time, including the covariance analysis.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
When the run finishes, a window opens with a summary figure of six panels: the 3D track with its 95th-percentile error tube, the 3D position error of every trial, the CEP with its linear fit, and the North tilt, East tilt and heading errors. Close the window to end the program.

It also saves the ground-track map, the app's Map tab, as maps/trajectory_map.html next to main.py. Open it in a web browser; the map tiles need an internet connection.

docs.title: Without a display
docs.text:
On a computer without a display, such as a server you log in to remotely, set the MPLBACKEND environment variable to Agg. The program then skips the summary window, with a warning that it cannot show it, and still saves the map:

MPLBACKEND=Agg python main.py --trials 100

For anything more, such as saving the numbers or looping over IMU specs, write a short script instead: see Your first script and Recipes.

docs.title: Modelling an IMU
docs.text: An IMU spec file describes how a unit's gyros and accelerometers err, in the units of a sensor datasheet. This page starts from three ready-made specs, one per grade of IMU, then shows how to enter your own sensor's datasheet. The IMU spec YAML reference lists every key, and the IMU error model page explains the mathematics.

docs.title: Three presets
docs.text:
Grade Typical use Gyro bias instability Accelerometer turn-on bias Navigation Airliners and ships, with ring-laser gyros 0.01 °/h 25 µg Tactical Missiles and large drones, with fibre-optic gyros 0.5 °/h 500 µg MEMS Small drones and vehicles, with silicon sensors 10 °/h 5,000 µg

The values are illustrative of each class; real products vary within it. The navigation-grade spec is the one the app ships with. To use another, copy it into a new .yaml file in the app's imu_specs folder (the copy button at the top right of each file copies it):

Navigation gradeTactical gradeMEMS 
name: Navigation-Grade RLG INS

# All values in datasheet units; load_imu_spec() converts to SI.
# Reference: typical ring-laser-gyro aircraft INS / marine-grade strapdown.

gyro:
  arw_deg_per_rt_hr:       0.002   # Angular Random Walk [°/√hr]
  bias_instab_deg_per_hr:  0.01    # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [°/hr]
  bias_tau_s:              3600.0  # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_deg_per_hr: 0.01   # Turn-on bias repeatability [°/hr]
  scale_factor_ppm:         5.0    # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:       50.0    # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad]

accel:
  vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr:   0.005   # Velocity Random Walk [m/s/√hr]
  bias_instab_ug:           5.0    # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [µg]
  bias_tau_s:              3600.0  # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_ug:         25.0   # Turn-on bias repeatability [µg]
  scale_factor_ppm:       100.0    # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:       50.0    # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad]

# Residual error of the stationary gyrocompass alignment, drawn once per
# Monte Carlo trial. Tilt ≈ accel repeatability / g; heading ≈ east-gyro
# repeatability / (Ω_ie·cos φ) — 0.04° corresponds to 0.01°/hr at ~18.5°N.
alignment:
  tilt_std_deg:    0.0015  # N/E tilt misalignment 1σ [°]
  heading_std_deg: 0.04    # Azimuth misalignment 1σ [°]

# Barometric altimeter that aids the vertical channel, typical of an
# aircraft air-data system. Omit this section for an ideal barometer.
# Near sea level 1 hPa of pressure is about 8.3 m of height.
baro:
  scale_factor_pct:   2.0     # Scale-factor error 1σ: a 6 K non-standard air temperature [%]
  bias_m:            10.0     # Static bias 1σ: altimeter-setting (QNH) error of about 1 hPa [m]
  drift_m:           10.0     # Weather drift 1σ: sea-level pressure changing en route [m]
  drift_tau_s:     7200.0     # Correlation time of the weather drift [s]
  noise_m_per_rt_hz:  0.1     # White-noise density [m/√Hz]

name: Tactical-Grade IMU

# Illustrative values for a tactical-grade IMU, such as a fibre-optic-gyro
# unit on a missile or a large drone: about 100 times less stable than the
# packaged navigation-grade spec. All values in datasheet units;
# load_imu_spec() converts them to SI.

gyro:
  arw_deg_per_rt_hr:        0.05    # Angular Random Walk [°/√hr]
  bias_instab_deg_per_hr:   0.5     # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [°/hr]
  bias_tau_s:               300.0   # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_deg_per_hr: 1.0     # Turn-on bias repeatability [°/hr]
  scale_factor_ppm:         100.0   # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:        100.0   # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad]

accel:
  vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr:    0.05    # Velocity Random Walk [m/s/√hr]
  bias_instab_ug:           50.0    # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [µg]
  bias_tau_s:               300.0   # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_ug:         500.0   # Turn-on bias repeatability [µg]
  scale_factor_ppm:         300.0   # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:        100.0   # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad]

# Tilt ≈ accel repeatability / g = 0.03°. Gyrocompassing with 1 °/hr gyros
# would leave about 4° of heading error at 18.5° N, so a tactical system
# takes its initial heading from elsewhere instead, here to 0.5°.
alignment:
  tilt_std_deg:    0.03    # N/E tilt misalignment 1σ [°]
  heading_std_deg: 0.5     # Azimuth misalignment 1σ [°]

name: Industrial MEMS IMU

# Illustrative values for an industrial-grade MEMS IMU, the kind found in
# drones and vehicle navigation units. Without aiding, from GNSS for
# example, it navigates for minutes rather than hours. All values in
# datasheet units; load_imu_spec() converts them to SI.

gyro:
  arw_deg_per_rt_hr:        0.3     # Angular Random Walk [°/√hr]
  bias_instab_deg_per_hr:   10.0    # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [°/hr]
  bias_tau_s:               100.0   # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_deg_per_hr: 20.0    # Turn-on bias left after a stationary startup calibration [°/hr]
  scale_factor_ppm:         2000.0  # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm] (0.2%)
  misalignment_urad:        1000.0  # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad] (1 mrad)

accel:
  vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr:    0.06    # Velocity Random Walk [m/s/√hr]
  bias_instab_ug:           50.0    # Bias instability, datasheet Allan-deviation floor [µg]
  bias_tau_s:               100.0   # Correlation time of the Gauss-Markov bias model [s]
  repeatability_ug:         5000.0  # Turn-on bias repeatability [µg] (5 mg)
  scale_factor_ppm:         2000.0  # Scale-factor error 1σ, per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:        1000.0  # Axis misalignment 1σ, per element [µrad]

# Tilt ≈ accel repeatability / g = 0.3°. These gyro biases are as large as
# the Earth's rotation rate (15 °/hr), so the gyros cannot find north;
# heading comes from a magnetometer instead, here to 2°.
alignment:
  tilt_std_deg:    0.3     # N/E tilt misalignment 1σ [°]
  heading_std_deg: 2.0     # Azimuth misalignment 1σ [°]

docs.title: How fast each grade drifts
docs.text:
This script flies the three specs through the half-hour training flight of Writing a mission:

"""How fast three grades of IMU lose position on the same flight."""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_imu_spec_path
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.evaluation.monte_carlo import run_monte_carlo
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import load_imu_spec
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

EXAMPLES = Path(__file__).parent
SPECS = {
    "Navigation": default_imu_spec_path(),
    "Tactical": EXAMPLES / "imu" / "tactical_grade.yaml",
    "MEMS": EXAMPLES / "imu" / "mems_grade.yaml",
}
MINUTES = [1, 5, 10, 25]


def distance(metres):
    """Formats a distance in metres below 1 km, in kilometres above."""
    return f"{metres:.0f} m" if metres < 1000 else f"{metres / 1000:.1f} km"


# A 2 s time step keeps the comparison quick: the grades differ far more
# than the time step changes the result.
truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(EXAMPLES / "missions" / "training_flight.yaml"),
                               tau_i=2.0)
samples = np.searchsorted(truth.t, [60.0 * m for m in MINUTES])

print("CEP of 10 trials on the training flight")
print(f"{'IMU grade':12s}" + "".join(f"{f'{m} min':>10s}" for m in MINUTES))
for grade, path in SPECS.items():
    spec = load_imu_spec(str(path))
    mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=10, seed=42)
    delta_r_eb_n = position_error(mc.est_L_b, mc.est_lambda_b, mc.est_h_b,
                                  truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)
    cep = np.median(np.hypot(delta_r_eb_n[..., 0], delta_r_eb_n[..., 1]), axis=0)
    print(f"{grade:12s}" + "".join(f"{distance(cep[k]):>10s}" for k in samples))

CEP of 10 trials on the training flight
IMU grade        1 min     5 min    10 min    25 min
Navigation         2 m      32 m     122 m     688 m
Tactical          22 m     534 m    2.9 km   27.6 km
MEMS             189 m    8.5 km   50.3 km  457.8 km

Each step down in grade costs more than an order of magnitude. After ten minutes the tactical-grade unit is about 25 times further off than the navigation-grade one, and the MEMS unit about 400 times. The MEMS unit is kilometres off within five minutes. That is why such units are always paired with GNSS or other aiding, which ins_sim does not model.

docs.title: From a datasheet to the YAML
docs.text:
Most datasheets give every value the spec needs, though not always in the same units:

Datasheet parameter YAML key Unit From other units Angle random walk (gyro noise) arw_deg_per_rt_hr °/√h °/√s or (°/s)/√Hz: × 60. (°/h)/√Hz: ÷ 60 Gyro bias instability bias_instab_deg_per_hr °/h °/s: × 3,600 Gyro turn-on bias repeatability repeatability_deg_per_hr °/h °/s: × 3,600 Velocity random walk (accelerometer noise) vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr m/s/√h µg/√Hz: × 0.000588. m/s/√s or (m/s²)/√Hz: × 60 Accelerometer bias instability bias_instab_ug µg mg: × 1,000 Accelerometer turn-on bias repeatability repeatability_ug µg mg: × 1,000 Scale-factor error scale_factor_ppm ppm %: × 10,000 Axis misalignment misalignment_urad µrad mrad: × 1,000. arcsec: × 4.848. °: × 17,453

Two more values rarely appear as numbers: the bias correlation time bias_tau_s, explained below, and the alignment block, which depends on how the system aligns rather than on the sensors alone.

Every spread is one standard deviation (1σ) per axis. If a datasheet gives a bound instead, convert it: divide a 3σ bound by three.

docs.title: Bias instability is the datasheet value
docs.text:
Enter the bias instability exactly as the datasheet gives it: the floor of the sensor's Allan deviation, the lowest point of its Allan-deviation plot. ins_sim models the wandering bias as a Gauss–Markov process and picks its spread so that the simulated sensor's Allan deviation peaks at exactly that value. The Validation page shows the match.

  • Some datasheets quote the IEEE 952 bias-instability coefficient instead of the floor. The floor is 0.664 times the coefficient, so multiply by 0.664 before entering it.
  • The correlation time bias_tau_s sets where the simulated Allan deviation peaks: at 1.89 times the correlation time. If the datasheet has an Allan-deviation plot, read off the averaging time \(T\) at the floor and enter \(T/1.89\). Without a plot you have to choose; the presets use one hour for navigation grade, 300 s for tactical grade and 100 s for MEMS.

docs.title: Turn-on bias and in-run bias
docs.text: The two bias terms behave differently in a run. The turn-on bias repeatability sets a constant bias, different every time the unit is switched on: ins_sim draws it once per trial. The bias instability sets how far the bias then wanders during the run. MEMS datasheets often call the turn-on value the initial bias error or bias repeatability, and the bias instability the in-run bias stability.

docs.title: Scale factor and misalignment
docs.text: A scale-factor error is a gain error: the sensor reads 100 ppm high, say. A misalignment means the sensor's axes are not exactly at right angles to each other and to the body. Both errors are proportional to what the sensors measure, so they never vanish. At rest the accelerometers still measure gravity, and a misaligned one reads part of it along a horizontal axis: the packaged spec's 50 µrad reads 50 µg, as much as a bias. In flight the errors grow with the turn rates and accelerations, so they matter most in manoeuvres. Each trial draws a scale factor per axis and six independent misalignment angles, two for each pair of axes.

docs.title: The alignment block
docs.text:
Before it navigates, an INS works out its initial attitude, and the alignment block gives how far off that is. It has two values: the tilt (about the North and East axes) and the heading error.

  • Self-alignment, for navigation grade. At rest, the unit levels itself by finding the direction of gravity, and finds North by sensing the Earth's rotation. The accelerometer bias limits the tilt and the gyro bias limits the heading. As a guide, the tilt in degrees is 0.000057 times the accelerometer turn-on bias in µg, and the heading error in degrees is about \(3.8\,b_g/\cos L_b\), with \(b_g\) the gyro turn-on bias in °/h and \(L_b\) the latitude.
  • Heading from elsewhere, for tactical grade and MEMS. With 1 °/h gyros, sensing the Earth's rotation would leave about 4° of heading error, and MEMS gyros, whose biases are as large as the Earth's rotation rate, cannot sense it usefully. These systems take their heading from a magnetometer, from GNSS, or from another navigator. Enter the accuracy of that source.

Leave the block out to start every trial from the true attitude. That is useful when you want to see the sensor errors alone.

docs.title: The baro block
docs.text:
With Baro altitude aiding on, a barometric altimeter holds the navigator's height (see Vertical channel). The baro block gives that altimeter's errors. A pressure altimeter turns pressure into height through a standard atmosphere, so most of its error comes from the day's atmosphere, not from the sensor. Near sea level, 1 hPa of pressure is about 8.3 m of height.

Key Error Where the packaged value comes from scale_factor_pct Air colder or warmer than standard: the altimeter's height above the departure point is off by this fraction 2%: about 6 K away from standard, out of 288 K bias_m The altimeter setting (QNH) and the sensor's offset, constant over a run 10 m: about 1 hPa drift_m, drift_tau_s The weather: sea-level pressure changing along the route and over time 10 m over about 2 hours noise_m_per_rt_hz Fast, random sensor noise 0.1 m/√Hz: 0.3 m per sample at 10 Hz

Whatever the barometer reports, the navigator's height follows within a couple of minutes, so these errors pass almost in full into the Down position error. On the packaged mission, which climbs to 4,600 m, the scale factor dominates: 2% of the climb is about 90 m. The horizontal errors hardly change.

Leave the block out for an ideal barometer that reports the true height. The tactical-grade and MEMS presets do that, so that comparing them compares the IMUs alone.

docs.title: Switching errors off
docs.text:
Set any value to 0 to remove that error. scale_factor_ppm, misalignment_urad, the alignment block and the baro block are optional and default to 0. Keep bias_tau_s positive, even when its bias instability is 0.

With every error at 0 the IMU is perfect, and the navigator follows the truth exactly. Switching errors off one group at a time shows which one matters most: see Recipes.

docs.title: What the model leaves out
docs.text: The model covers the errors that dominate a navigation-grade INS. It does not include g-dependent gyro bias, quantization, rate random walk, scale-factor nonlinearity, temperature effects or vibration. The IMU error model page lists these and the model's other assumptions.

docs.title: Writing a mission
docs.text: A mission file describes a flight the way a pilot would plan it: where it departs, then a list of phases (take-off, climbs, legs to waypoints, holding patterns, speed changes) in feet, knots and degrees. The simulator flies the plan smoothly, and the result becomes the truth that every Monte Carlo trial tries to follow. This page builds an example mission and explains how the simulator flies each part. The Mission YAML reference lists every key.

docs.title: Start from a copy
docs.text:
Mission files are plain text in the YAML format. Open the app's trajectories folder (see User guide), copy bqn_departure.yaml or the example below to a new name, and edit it in any text editor. It appears in the app's Trajectory list the next time you open the list.

Three rules of YAML matter here: indent with spaces, never tabs; start each list item, here each phase, with a dash; and anything after a # is a comment.

docs.title: An example: a training flight
docs.text:
This half-hour flight from Rafael Hernández Airport (BQN) uses every kind of phase:

name: BQN Training Flight

# A half-hour flight from Rafael Hernández Airport (BQN), Puerto Rico: climb
# to 8,000 ft, two turns in a holding pattern off the north coast, then a
# descent to 3,000 ft and a low-level leg east along the coast.

departure:
  lat_deg:  18.4949
  lon_deg: -67.1294
  alt_ft:   237.0              # runway elevation
  nav_bank_angle_deg: 25.0     # bank angle for the turns onto each leg

simulation_time:
  dt_s: 0.1                    # used only when a script gives no time step

phases:

  - type:           ground_roll  # from rest to lift-off speed
    heading_deg:    82.0
    run_length_m:   1800.0
    speed_final_kt: 150.0

  - type:        takeoff         # rotate to 10° pitch while accelerating
    heading_deg: 82.0
    pitch_deg:   10.0
    speed_kt:    220.0
    duration_s:  20.0

  - type:           climb        # straight ahead to cruise altitude
    pitch_deg:      8.0
    speed_kt:       220.0
    to_altitude_ft: 8000.0

  - type:     waypoint           # hold off the north coast
    lat_deg:  18.80
    lon_deg:  -66.70
    alt_ft:   8000.0
    speed_kt: 240.0
    loiter:
      n_turns:        2
      bank_angle_deg: 25.0
      direction:      left

  - type:         speed_ramp
    speed_end_kt: 280.0
    duration_s:   30.0

  - type:     waypoint           # descend to 3,000 ft on the way
    lat_deg:  18.75
    lon_deg:  -66.20
    alt_ft:   3000.0

  - type:     waypoint           # low-level leg east along the coast
    lat_deg:  18.55
    lon_deg:  -65.80
    alt_ft:   3000.0

The file has four parts:

  • name is for your reference; the app lists missions by file name.
  • departure is the starting point, on the runway, and the bank angle for the turns onto each leg. The runway elevation is in feet above mean sea level.
  • simulation_time holds a time step that only a Python script uses, and only when it gives no time step of its own. The app and the command line always use their own setting.
  • phases lists the flight, in order. Each phase starts where the previous one ended, with its position, heading, speed and altitude.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
Phase What the aircraft does ground_roll Accelerates from rest along the runway heading, reaching speed_final_kt after run_length_m metres. Every mission starts with one, and only one. takeoff Pitches up from level to pitch_deg over duration_s seconds, on heading_deg, while the speed changes to speed_kt. Give it the runway heading. climb Climbs straight ahead at speed_kt, at a flight-path angle of pitch_deg, to to_altitude_ft. If the target is lower, it descends at that angle instead. waypoint Turns toward the fix at lat_deg, lon_deg, then flies straight to it, climbing or descending steadily to alt_ft on the way. speed_kt sets the leg's speed; without it the aircraft keeps its current speed. An optional loiter block then flies n_turns full circles at bank_angle_deg, to the right (the default) or left. speed_ramp Changes speed steadily, over duration_s seconds, to speed_end_kt or to the Mach number speed_end_mach, keeping heading and altitude.

A Mach number is converted to a speed with the speed of sound of the International Standard Atmosphere at the altitude of the last climb or waypoint: Mach 0.8 at 15,000 ft is 501 kt.

docs.title: Check a mission before running it
docs.text:
The quickest check is in the app: run 2 trials at a 1 s time step and look at the 3D Trajectory and Map tabs. The log also reports the mission's length and duration.

For more detail, this script flies a mission and reports its duration, distance, limits, and how close the track passes each waypoint:

"""Checks a mission before a Monte Carlo run: how long, how far, how close to each waypoint."""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import yaml

from ins_sim.core.earth_model import wgs84_radii
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

MISSION = Path(__file__).parent / "missions" / "training_flight.yaml"
FT, KT, NM = 0.3048, 0.514444, 1852.0

truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(MISSION), tau_i=1.0)

speed = np.linalg.norm(truth.v_eb_n, axis=1)
flown = np.sum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(truth.r_lb_l, axis=0), axis=1))
print(f"Duration           {truth.t[-1] / 60:7.1f} min")
print(f"Distance flown     {flown / NM:7.1f} nmi")
print(f"Highest altitude   {truth.h_b.max() / FT:7.0f} ft")
print(f"Top speed          {speed.max() / KT:7.0f} kt")
print(f"Steepest bank      {np.rad2deg(np.abs(truth.euler_nb[:, 0])).max():7.1f} deg")
print(f"Steepest pitch     {np.rad2deg(np.abs(truth.euler_nb[:, 1])).max():7.1f} deg")

# How close the track passes each waypoint, from the latitude and longitude
# differences converted to metres with the WGS-84 radii of curvature.
with open(MISSION, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    waypoints = [p for p in yaml.safe_load(fh)["phases"] if p["type"] == "waypoint"]
for n, wp in enumerate(waypoints, start=1):
    L_wp, lambda_wp = np.deg2rad(wp["lat_deg"]), np.deg2rad(wp["lon_deg"])
    R_N, R_E = wgs84_radii(L_wp)
    north = (truth.L_b - L_wp) * R_N
    east = (truth.lambda_b - lambda_wp) * R_E * np.cos(L_wp)
    k = np.argmin(np.hypot(north, east))
    print(f"Waypoint {n}: passes {np.hypot(north[k], east[k]) / 1000:4.1f} km away "
          f"at {truth.t[k] / 60:4.1f} min, at {truth.h_b[k] / FT:5.0f} ft "
          f"(planned {wp['alt_ft']:.0f} ft)")

For the training flight it prints:

Duration              27.0 min
Distance flown       112.7 nmi
Highest altitude      8030 ft
Top speed              280 kt
Steepest bank         25.0 deg
Steepest pitch         8.9 deg
Waypoint 1: passes  0.1 km away at 14.6 min, at  8030 ft (planned 8000 ft)
Waypoint 2: passes  3.0 km away at 21.2 min, at  3433 ft (planned 3000 ft)
Waypoint 3: passes  0.8 km away at 26.9 min, at  3037 ft (planned 3000 ft)

The aircraft passes right over the first waypoint, where its holding pattern starts, and within a kilometre of the last one. It misses the second by 3 km, for a reason the next section explains, and so passes it at 3,433 ft, still descending: its closest point to the waypoint comes before the end of the leg, which reaches 3,000 ft later. At the other two waypoints the altitudes are 30–40 ft high because of the 1 s time step; at 0.1 s they are within a few feet.

docs.title: How the simulator flies a plan
docs.text:
The simulator turns the plan into a smooth flight that obeys the laws of motion, rather than one that passes exactly through every point:

  • Turns. The aircraft turns onto each leg at the departure's nav_bank_angle_deg, in a coordinated turn: the bank angle follows from the speed and the turn rate, and there is no sideslip.
  • Waypoints are approached, not hit. The bearing and distance to a waypoint are worked out from where the previous phase ended, before the turn onto the leg. The turn moves the aircraft sideways, so after a large turn the leg runs parallel to the planned one, offset by up to the turn's diameter: about 9 km at 280 kt and 25° of bank. The leg is then flown at a constant heading, which drifts from the great circle on long legs, by about 11 km over 1,000 km. On the packaged mission the track passes 3.5 to 5.6 km from each waypoint. To pass closer, add an intermediate waypoint so that the turn before the final leg is small.
  • Climbs and descents on a leg are steady. A waypoint leg changes altitude at a constant angle, set by the leg's length. A short leg with a large altitude change therefore makes a steep climb or dive: a 3° descent needs about 19 km for every 1,000 m.
  • Speed changes belong in a speed_ramp. A waypoint's speed_kt takes effect at the end of its turn, so a large change there is abrupt.
  • Transitions are smoothed. The velocity is smoothed over about two seconds, so the bank and pitch change over a few seconds at every phase boundary, as in a real aircraft.
  • Altitudes are close, not exact. Each change of phase can leave the altitude off by up to one time step's worth of climb: a few tens of feet at a 1 s time step, a few feet at 0.1 s.
  • What is not modelled. There is no wind, no angle of attack (the pitch equals the flight-path angle) and no sideslip. Heights are measured from the WGS-84 ellipsoid, and the departure elevation is used as such, since ins_sim has no geoid model.

The Truth trajectory & ideal IMU page explains how the flown plan becomes the truth and the perfect IMU outputs.

docs.title: When a mission fails to load
docs.text:
A mission that does not appear in the Trajectory list either has a YAML syntax error (often a tab, or a missing colon or dash) or has no phases section. Browse… says so when you pick it.

A mission that appears but has a mistake stops the run with a Simulation failed message:

Message Cause ValueError: The first phase must be a 'ground_roll'... The first phase is something else, or the phases are out of order. ValueError: Only the first phase can be a 'ground_roll' A second ground_roll: there is only one take-off run. ValueError: Unknown phase type: 'clmb' A misspelt phase type. KeyError: 'speed_kt' A phase lacks a required key, here speed_kt. The reference lists each phase's keys. ValueError: speed_end_mach needs an earlier 'climb' or 'waypoint' phase... A Mach speed_ramp before any phase has set the altitude. KeyError: 'simulation_time' The simulation_time section is missing.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Short answers to questions that come up once the simulator is running. Most need only the app; the error budget also has a script.

docs.title: Get a quick answer, then a precise one
docs.text: Explore with 10 trials at a 1 s time step: the packaged mission then runs in about 15 seconds, quick enough to try several missions or IMU specs. Once you know what you want to show, rerun it at the defaults, 50 trials at 0.1 s, or with more trials (see below) for the final numbers.

docs.title: Choose the time step
docs.text:
The time step decides how finely the truth and the navigator are sampled; the run time is proportional to the number of steps. It hardly changes how fast the errors grow, because that comes from the sensor errors, not from the sampling. On the packaged mission, 50 trials give a CEP growth of 1.24 nmi/h at a 1 s step and 1.28 nmi/h at 0.1 s, and ±3σ bands that end within 10% of each other.

A 1 s step is therefore fine for studying error growth over tens of minutes. Use 0.1 s, the default and the setting of the figures in these docs, for final numbers and for short, fast manoeuvres.

docs.title: How many trials?
docs.text:
Every statistic comes from a finite sample of trials, and is uncertain accordingly:

Trials Uncertainty of a ±3σ band Good for 10 about 25% a first look at the shape of the errors 50 about 10% the CEP and the ±3σ bands: the default 200 about 5% the 95th percentile, the 3D tube and the map band

The 95th percentile needs the most trials, because it rests on the few worst ones: with 50 trials, on the worst two or three. The Monte Carlo evaluation page derives these numbers.

docs.title: Compare two IMUs fairly
docs.text:
Run both specs on the same mission with the same time step and number of trials. The app always uses the same random seed, and every error is drawn the same way whatever its size. The two runs therefore use the same underlying random numbers, scaled by each spec's values, so the difference between them comes from the specs, not from luck. This makes the difference between two specs much more precise than either result on its own, even with few trials.

The same holds for any other change to the IMU spec, such as the alignment block, as long as the mission and the time step stay the same. Changing either of those changes the number of samples, and with it the noise: each trial keeps its turn-on biases, scale factors, misalignments and alignment errors, but its noise is drawn afresh. Comparisons between missions therefore need more trials. In a script, pass the same seed to run_monte_carlo.

docs.title: Find the dominant error source
docs.text:
To find which error limits a navigator, read the Error Budget tab after a run (see Reading the results). It comes from a covariance analysis, which predicts the error of each source on its own without random trials, so it has no sampling noise even for a source whose contribution is small.

In a script, error_budget gives the same numbers:

"""Which error source dominates? The covariance analysis's error budget for the training flight."""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_imu_spec_path
from ins_sim.evaluation.covariance import error_budget
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.evaluation.monte_carlo import run_monte_carlo
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import load_imu_spec
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

MISSION = Path(__file__).parent / "missions" / "training_flight.yaml"

truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(MISSION), tau_i=2.0)
spec = load_imu_spec(str(default_imu_spec_path()))
budget = error_budget(truth, spec)


def horizontal_variance(part):
    """North plus East position variance at the end of the flight [m²]."""
    return part.var[-1, 6] + part.var[-1, 7]


print(f"After {truth.t[-1] / 60:.0f} min        CEP alone   share of the variance")
for source, part in budget.by_source.items():
    share = 100 * horizontal_variance(part) / horizontal_variance(budget.total)
    print(f"  {source:38s} {part.cep[-1]:5.0f} m   {share:5.1f}%")
print(f"  {'All sources together':38s} {budget.total.cep[-1]:5.0f} m")

# The same flight, flown 50 times with random errors.
mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=50, seed=42)
delta_r_eb_n = position_error(mc.est_L_b, mc.est_lambda_b, mc.est_h_b,
                              truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)
cep = np.median(np.hypot(delta_r_eb_n[:, -1, 0], delta_r_eb_n[:, -1, 1]))
print(f"  {'Monte Carlo, 50 trials':38s} {cep:5.0f} m")

On the half-hour training flight of Writing a mission it prints:

After 27 min        CEP alone   share of the variance
  Initial alignment                        395 m    30.0%
  Gyro biases                              430 m    31.8%
  Gyro scale factor and misalignment       218 m     9.0%
  Accelerometer biases                     182 m     5.7%
  Accel. scale factor and misalignment     347 m    20.8%
  Sensor noise (ARW and VRW)               125 m     2.7%
  Barometer                                  3 m     0.0%
  All sources together                     759 m
  Monte Carlo, 50 trials                   796 m

On this flight the initial alignment and the gyro biases dominate, with the accelerometer scale factors and misalignments next: the training flight's climbs and turns load them more than the packaged mission does. A better accelerometer bias would barely help, while a better alignment or better gyros would. The barometer aids only the height, so it hardly touches the horizontal CEP. The CEPs of single sources do not add up to the total; their shares of the variance do. The prediction of all sources together agrees with the 50 trials to within their sampling uncertainty.

To check a budget with trials, run the Monte Carlo with one group of errors at a time, setting every other value to 0 as described in Modelling an IMU. Each group draws exactly the same errors as in the run with every error on (see above), but a single source needs many trials: with 10, the CEP of one source can be off by a factor of two.

Which source dominates depends on the flight: errors that the Schuler oscillation keeps bounded, such as the accelerometer biases, matter less on long flights than errors that keep growing, such as the gyro biases. Rerun the budget for your own mission; the INS error model page explains how each error grows.

docs.title: Check that a mission flies as planned
docs.text: Run it with 2 trials at a 1 s step and look at the 3D Trajectory and Map tabs, or use the checking script in Writing a mission.

docs.title: Fly a path of your own from Python
docs.text: A mission file is not the only way to make a truth trajectory. TruthTrajectory.from_spline flies a smooth path through a list of points at constant speed, and run_monte_carlo accepts the result like any other. See its example on the Trajectory page of the Python API.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text: After a run, the app shows one tab per result. Each tab summarizes all the trials: how far the navigator's estimates drifted from the truth, and how much that drift varies from one set of sensor errors to another. The figures on this page come from the packaged mission and IMU spec at the app's default settings: 50 trials at a 0.1 s time step.

docs.title: What every tab has in common
docs.text:
• An error is the estimate minus the truth. A positive North position error means the navigator thinks it is north of where it really is.
  • Errors are measured along North, East and Down at the true position. Position errors are in metres; the latitude, longitude and height errors are converted to distances along those three directions.
  • Bands are ±3σ. Where a tab shows a band, it is centred on the average error over the trials and extends three standard deviations each side of it. For normally distributed errors it holds 99.7% of the trials.
  • Percentiles count trials. The CEP is the 50th percentile of the horizontal error: half the trials are within it. The tube and the map band use the 95th percentile.
  • Dashed crimson lines are predictions. After the trials, the app runs a covariance analysis, which predicts the spread of the errors without random trials. The CEP, attitude, velocity and position tabs draw it as dashed lines: the predicted CEP, and ±3σ about zero. Where the trials' band and the dashed lines part, the trials are too few, or the errors too large for the prediction's linear model.

The Monte Carlo evaluation page gives the exact definitions.

docs.title: Working with the plots
docs.text:
Every tab is an interactive plot. Hover to read values. Drag a box or scroll to zoom, and double-click to zoom back out. Click a legend entry to hide or show it. In the 3D view, drag to rotate. The camera icon at the top right saves the plot as a PNG image.

Axis labels use SI prefixes: k for thousands and M for millions, so 10k m is 10 km.

docs.title: CEP
docs.text:
Each faint line is one trial's horizontal position error, in nautical miles (NM), against time in hours.

  • The dashed line is a straight-line fit to the CEP over the first hour, marked by the dotted line. Its slope, 1.28 nmi/h here, is the usual figure of merit of an INS. The line starts slightly below zero because the errors grow slowly at first.
  • The dashed crimson line is the CEP the covariance analysis predicts.
  • Under the plot, a table gives the 50th percentile (the CEP), the 95th percentile of the horizontal error and the predicted CEP at each whole hour of flight. Flights shorter than an hour have no table.

The trials fan out because each one has different sensor errors. One unlucky trial here ends 6.6 nmi off while others end within 0.5 nmi, which is why the CEP and the 95th percentile, not a single run, describe the navigator.

docs.title: Attitude Errors
docs.text:
The attitude error is the small rotation that would turn the true attitude into the estimated one, split into three angles: the North tilt and East tilt, about the horizontal axes, and the heading error, about the vertical. Unlike differences of roll, pitch and heading, these three angles mean the same thing whatever the aircraft's attitude. The Frames & attitude page defines them.

  • The tilts stay below about 0.03° (3σ). Each wobble in the bands comes from a turn of the holding patterns, at about 10–22 and 47–61 minutes.
  • The heading error starts at the alignment spread, 0.12° (3σ), and grows in steps during the holding patterns, where the gyros' axis misalignments act on the turn rate. It barely changes on the straight legs. The INS error model explains how heading error turns into position error.

docs.title: Velocity Errors
docs.text:
The North and East velocity errors grow to a few metres per second, but not steadily. An INS's velocity errors oscillate with an 84-minute period, the Schuler period, so the bands swell and shrink: on this flight the North band peaks at about an hour and then narrows. The INS error model page explains the oscillation.

The Down velocity error reaches about ±1.5 m/s during the climb, while the navigator follows the barometer's height error as it grows, and then stays within about 0.2 m/s, held by the barometric loop.

docs.title: Position Errors
docs.text:
The position errors are the integral of the velocity errors. By the end of the 80-minute flight the bands reach about ±10 km North and ±5 km East. The Down band grows to about ±250 m during the climb and then stays there. That is the barometer's error, which the navigator's height follows: mostly its temperature scale factor, which grows with the height above the departure point (see Modelling an IMU). Without baro aiding the Down error grows exponentially instead; see Your first simulation.

The average error, the dark line, stays near zero in all three panels, because every sensor error is as likely to be positive as negative. What matters for one flight is the spread.

docs.title: 3D Trajectory
docs.text:
The truth track (black), every trial's estimated track (faint blue), and a red tube around the truth whose radius is the 95th percentile of the 3D position error. Distances are in kilometres from the starting point, East, North and Up.

The axes are not to the same scale: the plot stretches the 4.5 km of climb to the same size as the 450 km the track spans from north to south. The tube, a circle around the track at every point, therefore looks like a tall, flat fin. Drag to rotate the view, or scroll to zoom into the climb.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
The ground track over OpenStreetMap: the true track (dark blue), each trial's estimated track (faint blue), and a red band whose half-width is the 95th percentile of the horizontal error. White dots mark every five minutes. Hover over the track to read the time and the 95th-percentile error at that point.

The background tiles need an internet connection; without one the tracks and the band appear on a blank background.

docs.title: Error Budget
docs.text:
Which error source limits the navigator? The covariance analysis predicts the error of each source on its own, and since its model is linear, their variances add up to the total. The plot stacks each source's share of the predicted horizontal position variance over the flight; the shares always fill 100%. Hover to read them at any time.

The table under the plot lists, at each whole hour of flight (or at the end, for a shorter flight), each source's predicted CEP on its own and its share of the variance, then the predicted CEP of all sources together. The CEPs of single sources do not add up to the total; their variances do.

On the packaged mission the initial alignment errors dominate the first few minutes, and the accelerometer scale factors and misalignments the climb-out. From about 15 minutes the gyro scale factors and misalignments, fed by every turn, take the largest share, and by the end the gyro biases have caught up with them. After the first half hour a better accelerometer would barely change the result; better gyros would. Recipes shows how to act on a budget.

docs.title: How many trials?
docs.text: The statistics are estimates from a finite number of trials. With 50 trials a standard deviation, and so a ±3σ band, is uncertain by about 10%, and the 95th percentile rests on the two or three worst trials. Recipes gives a rule of thumb, and the Monte Carlo evaluation page the details.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to ins_sim. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and the version numbers Semantic Versioning: before 1.0, a new minor version may change the API.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • A running simulation can be cancelled. While a run is active, the Run Simulation button becomes Cancel; click it or press Esc to stop the run after the current trial. The app then offers to show the results of the trials that finished; if you decline, the previous results stay on screen. In Python, run_monte_carlo takes should_stop, a callable that ends the run early and returns the trials completed so far. (#18)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The app no longer fills the temp folder with plot pages. Each session wrote its plots and a 4.5 MB copy of plotly.js to a new temp folder and never removed it. The app now deletes its folder when it quits, and on start it removes the folders that earlier sessions left behind, including those from older versions. A folder that another open window is still using is left alone. (#11)
  • Closing the window during a run no longer crashes the app. The app asks whether to stop the simulation; if you agree, it stops after the current trial and then closes. (#10)

Version 0.4.0 makes the simulation more realistic and adds a second way to evaluate a navigator: a barometer that errs like a real one, a precision navigation algorithm for testing the algorithm itself, and a covariance analysis that predicts the errors and splits them by source without random trials. The Python API only grows: code written for 0.3.0 runs unchanged. The app's default results change, because the packaged IMU spec now has a barometer (see Changed).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A barometer error model. The barometric altimeter that aids the vertical channel now errs like a real one: a scale-factor error from non-standard air temperature, a static bias from the altimeter setting, a weather drift and white noise. An optional baro block in the IMU spec sets them; without it the barometer is ideal, as before. In Python, IMUSpec.baro takes a BaroSpec, and generate_baro_samples draws the measurements. Each trial draws its barometer errors from a random stream of its own, so they leave the IMU and alignment errors unchanged.
  • A precision mechanization and an integrating IMU, to test the navigation algorithm itself. strapdown_navgrade(..., mechanization="precision") adds coning, rotation and sculling corrections and a trapezoidal position update. build_trajectory(..., oversample=M) and TruthTrajectory(..., oversample=M) build the truth M times per IMU interval and give the IMU outputs as averages over each interval, as a real integrating IMU reports them. run_monte_carlo takes mechanization too; the app has both under Advanced, and main.py has --mechanization and --oversample. Both default to the previous behaviour, which gives the same results as before.
  • A covariance analysis and an error budget. covariance_analysis propagates the covariance of a 43-state linearized error model, with every error source of the simulator as a state, along the truth trajectory: it predicts the spread of the attitude, velocity and position errors and the CEP in one pass. error_budget gives each error source's share. The app draws the prediction as dashed lines on the CEP, attitude, velocity and position tabs and has a new Error Budget tab; main.py prints the budget. The Monte Carlo results are unchanged.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The packaged IMU spec has a barometer, typical of an aircraft air-data system, so the app's default results differ from 0.3.0. The Down position error on the packaged mission grows from under 10 m to about 80 m (1σ); the horizontal errors barely change. IMU specs that the app has already copied into your imu_specs folder keep their ideal barometer; add a baro block to them, or copy the new default, to get the new behaviour.

Version 0.3.0 adopts the notation of Groves, Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems (2nd ed., 2013), in the code and the documentation, measures and models the navigation errors more carefully, and adds complete documentation. The Python API changes, and results differ from 0.2.0. The Migrating from 0.2 guide lists every change.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The Python API is renamed after the Groves symbols. For example, pos_n becomes r_lb_l, lat, lon and alt become L_b, lambda_b and h_b, R_b2n becomes C_b_n, omega_b and f_b become omega_ib_b and f_ib_b, and dt becomes tau_i. The radii of curvature become R_N (meridian) and R_E (transverse): in 0.2, R_N was the transverse radius. Functions that returned tuples return named tuples.
  • run_monte_carlo returns a MonteCarloResult with seven fields, including the new est_h_b and delta_psi_nb_n, and percentile_envelope takes the position-error array.
  • Bias instability is the datasheet value: the floor of the sensor's Allan deviation. The spread of the in-run bias is derived from it so that the simulated Allan deviation peaks there; for the same IMU spec, it is 1.62 times the spread of 0.2. IMUSpec.gyro_bi_std and accel_bi_std become gyro_bias_instability and accel_bias_instability, with the spreads as the new properties gyro_gm_std and accel_gm_std.
  • Attitude errors are the small rotation between the estimated and true attitude, as North tilt, East tilt and heading error, instead of differences of roll, pitch and heading. The app's Attitude Errors tab and the command-line summary show them.
  • Position errors are the latitude, longitude and height errors in metres along North, East and Down at the true position, in every result.
  • The in-run bias starts at its steady-state spread instead of zero.
  • Each trial draws its alignment, gyro and accelerometer errors from separate random streams, so changing one error source leaves the others' draws unchanged. The same seed draws different errors than in 0.2.
  • The ±3σ bands use the sample standard deviation (dividing by N − 1).
  • ins_sim requires NumPy 1.25 or later.
  • The Linux downloads use the system's own libraries for graphics, fonts, sound and encryption, like other desktop apps, instead of copies from the machine that built them.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Documentation, with a version selector: tutorials for the app and for Python, a user guide, the theory and mathematics of every part of the simulator, a validation of the simulator against textbook results, the Python API reference, references for the mission and IMU-spec files, and a glossary and bibliography.
  • IMU specs for a tactical-grade and a MEMS unit, and an example mission, in the documentation.
  • ins_sim.evaluation.errors, with the three error definitions: attitude_error, velocity_error and position_error.
  • Runnable examples in the docstrings.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Missions can descend. A waypoint leg to a lower altitude used to stay level, and a climb phase to a lower altitude climbed.
  • A mission whose first phase is not a ground_roll fails with a clear message instead of cannot convert float NaN to integer.
  • The stated accuracy of the gravity model's height correction.
  • The downloadable app leaves out the Qt modules it does not use, some of which Qt offers only under the GPL-3.0, so the downloads are smaller.
  • The license notices in the downloadable app also credit the Python runtime, PyInstaller's launcher, Microsoft's runtime libraries (Windows), ICU (Linux), and the GCC libraries in NumPy and SciPy.
  • When Qt WebEngine cannot load, the result tabs say why, naming the missing system library, instead of asking to reinstall PySide6. The download page lists the libraries the Linux ARM64 build needs.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A Linux ARM64 build, for the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 running the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS.
  • trajectories and imu_specs folders next to the app, holding copies of the packaged files. Missions and IMU specs saved there appear in the app's lists, and Browse… opens them.
  • A documentation site: download and installation, a user guide and the theory, illustrated with figures produced by the simulator.
  • Third-party license notices and texts in the downloadable app.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • A smaller downloadable app: packages the app does not use are left out.

The first release.

  • A desktop app: choose a mission and an IMU spec, run a Monte Carlo ensemble in the background, and explore interactive results: the CEP with an hourly percentile table, the attitude, velocity and position errors with ±3σ bands, a 3D trajectory with its 95th-percentile error tube, and a ground-track map.
  • An IMU error model with angle and velocity random walk, Gauss–Markov bias drift, turn-on bias, scale-factor and misalignment errors, and initial alignment errors.
  • A baro-damped or free-inertial vertical channel.
  • A command-line run with a summary figure and an interactive map.
  • Downloadable apps for Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Migrating from 0.2
docs.text: Version 0.3 renames the Python API after the symbols of Groves (2013), measures and models the navigation errors more carefully, and reads bias instability as the datasheet value. Mission and IMU files load as before, and the app works the same way, but the results differ from 0.2, and Python scripts need updating.

docs.title: Results change
docs.text:
Each of these changes alters the numbers you get from the same files:

Change Effect Bias instability is the datasheet value, the floor of the Allan deviation. 0.2 used it directly as the spread of the in-run bias. The in-run bias spread is 1.62 times that of 0.2 for the same file. See Modelling an IMU. The in-run bias starts at its full spread. In 0.2 it started at zero and grew over its correlation time. Larger errors early in a flight. Attitude errors are the small rotation between the estimated and true attitude, as North tilt, East tilt and heading error. 0.2 plotted differences of roll, pitch and heading. A different Attitude Errors tab; its checkbox, formerly Attitude/Euler Angle Errors, is renamed. Position errors are the latitude, longitude and height errors in metres along North, East and Down at the true position, in every result. 0.2 subtracted positions relative to the starting point. The two agree near the start and differ more the further the flight goes. Each trial draws its alignment, gyro and accelerometer errors from three separate random streams. The same seed draws different errors than in 0.2. The ±3σ bands use the sample standard deviation (dividing by N − 1). Slightly wider bands with few trials. Missions can descend. In 0.2 a waypoint leg to a lower altitude stayed level, and a climb to a lower altitude climbed. Missions with descents now fly as written. A mission must start with a ground_roll. 0.2 crashed on such a file with an obscure error. A clear error message instead.

docs.title: Mission and IMU files
docs.text:
The keys are unchanged, so every 0.2 file loads in 0.3. One value changes meaning: bias_instab_deg_per_hr and bias_instab_ug are now read as the datasheet bias instability.

  • If you took them from a datasheet, there is nothing to do: 0.3 now simulates them as the datasheet means them.
  • If you had tuned them as the spread of the in-run bias, as 0.2 used them, multiply them by 0.617 to keep the same simulated bias.

The app never overwrites the files in its imu_specs folder, so the copy of imu_spec.yaml it made under 0.2 keeps comments that describe bias instability as a Gauss–Markov spread. Its values are those of 0.3's packaged spec. To get the new comments, delete the copy and restart the app, which makes a fresh one.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Physics quantities are named after their symbols: v_eb_n is the velocity \(\vvec{eb}{n}\), C_b_n the attitude \(\Cmat{b}{n}\). The Notation & conventions page lists each symbol with its 0.2 name. In practice:

  • Function names are unchanged, but many argument names change. Calls that pass arguments by position keep working; keyword arguments need the new names.
  • Functions that returned a tuple now return a named tuple. Unpacking by position works as before, except for run_monte_carlo, which now returns seven fields, and every field can also be read by name.
  • ins_sim now needs NumPy 1.25 or later.

docs.title: Earth model
docs.text:
0.2 0.3 wgs84_radii(lat) returned (R_M, R_N) wgs84_radii(L_b) returns Radii(R_N, R_E) earth_rate_n(lat) earth_rate_n(L_b) transport_rate_n(v_n, lat, h) transport_rate_n(v_eb_n, L_b, h_b) normal_gravity(lat, h) normal_gravity(L_b, h_b)

R_N changed meaning

0.2 called the meridian radius of curvature R_M and the transverse one R_N. 0.3 follows Groves: R_N is the meridian radius and R_E the transverse one. wgs84_radii still returns the meridian radius first, so R_M, R_N = wgs84_radii(lat) still runs, but its R_N is now what the docs call R_E. Rename it to avoid confusion.

docs.title: Trajectory
docs.text:
0.2 0.3 build_trajectory(yaml_path, dt=None) build_trajectory(yaml_path, tau_i=None), returning MissionTrajectory(truth, v_sprint, R_turn) TruthTrajectory(pos_n, vel_n, euler, dt, lat0_deg, lon0_deg, alt0) TruthTrajectory(pos_profile, v_eb_n, euler_nb, tau_i, L_b0_deg, lambda_b0_deg, h_b0) TruthTrajectory.from_spline(path, speed, dt, lat0_deg, lon0_deg, alt0) TruthTrajectory.from_spline(path, speed, tau_i, L_b0_deg, lambda_b0_deg, h_b0)

The truth trajectory's attributes:

docs.title: Bibliography
docs.text:
Works cited in these pages. Equation and section numbers quoted from Groves always refer to the second edition (2013); the first edition (2008) numbers its equations differently.

These docs follow Groves' notation. Every derivation, figure and table here is written fresh, and none is reproduced from the book.

Savage, "Strapdown inertial navigation integration algorithm design, part 2: Velocity and position algorithms," Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, vol. 21, no. 2, pp. 208–221, 1998.
