docs.title: IMU error model
docs.text:
Gyros and accelerometers are never perfect. Each output carries a bias that differs every time the IMU is switched on and wanders slowly during a run, gain and alignment errors that grow with the motion, and white noise. The navigator integrates all of these, which is why an INS drifts. The IMU spec you choose in the GUI sets the size of each error, in the units of a sensor datasheet. ins_sim models them with the sensor error model of Groves1, one realization per Monte Carlo trial.

Key results

  • Each sensor output is the true value, scaled and cross-coupled by a matrix \(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}\), plus a static bias, a slowly varying dynamic bias and white noise.
  • Bias instability is entered as the datasheet value \(B\). The dynamic bias is a Gauss–Markov process with spread \(B/0.617\), so that its Allan deviation peaks at exactly \(B\).
  • The white noise per sample is the random-walk density divided by \(\sqrt{\tau_i}\), so results do not depend on the IMU's sample rate.
  • Every trial draws its own errors, from separate random streams for the gyros, the accelerometers and the initial alignment.

docs.title: Physical picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T["True rate ω<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup><br/>or specific force f<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>"] --> M["× (I + M)<br/>scale factor and<br/>misalignment"]
    M --> S["+ static bias<br/>b<sub>s</sub>"]
    S --> D["+ dynamic bias<br/>b<sub>d</sub>(t)"]
    D --> W["+ white noise<br/>w"]
    W --> O["Sensor output"]

The error terms behave very differently:

  • Scale factor and misalignment. A sensor's gain is slightly wrong, by parts per million, and its axes are not exactly orthogonal or exactly along the body axes, by microradians. These errors are proportional to what the sensor measures, so they are present even at rest, where the accelerometers measure gravity and the gyros the Earth's rotation, and largest in turns and accelerations.
  • Static bias. Every time the IMU is switched on, each bias settles at a slightly different value, then stays there for the run. Datasheets call its spread the turn-on bias repeatability.
  • Dynamic bias. During the run the bias wanders slowly, over minutes to hours. Datasheets quantify this as the bias instability.
  • White noise. Every sample is noisy. Integrated by the navigator, gyro noise becomes a random walk in angle (angle random walk, ARW) and accelerometer noise a random walk in velocity (VRW).

The packaged spec is typical of a ring-laser-gyro aircraft INS:

Error Gyro Accelerometer YAML keys Random walk 0.002 °/√h 0.005 m/s/√h arw_deg_per_rt_hr, vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr Bias instability (datasheet) 0.01 °/h 5 µg bias_instab_deg_per_hr, bias_instab_ug Bias correlation time 1 h 1 h bias_tau_s Turn-on bias repeatability 0.01 °/h 25 µg repeatability_deg_per_hr, repeatability_ug Scale factor 5 ppm 100 ppm scale_factor_ppm Misalignment 50 µrad 50 µrad misalignment_urad

and its initial alignment leaves a tilt of 0.0015° and a heading error of 0.04° (1σ), set in its alignment: block.

docs.title: The measurement equations
docs.text:
\[ \fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_a + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_a\right)\fvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_a, \qquad \wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_g + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_g\right)\wvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_g \]

where:

  • \(\fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\) and \(\wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\) are the accelerometer and gyro outputs [m/s², rad/s], and \(\fvec{ib}{b}\), \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) the true specific force and angular rate (see Truth trajectory & ideal IMU);
  • \(\mathbf{b}_a = \mathbf{b}_{as} + \mathbf{b}_{ad}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_g = \mathbf{b}_{gs} + \mathbf{b}_{gd}\) are the biases, each a static part (subscript s) and a dynamic part (subscript d) [m/s², rad/s];
  • \(\mathbf{M}_a\) and \(\mathbf{M}_g\) are the scale-factor and misalignment matrices [dimensionless];
  • \(\mathbf{w}_a\) and \(\mathbf{w}_g\) are white noise [m/s², rad/s].

docs.title: Scale factor and misalignment
docs.text:
\[ \mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & m_{xy} & m_{xz} \\ m_{yx} & s_y & m_{yz} \\ m_{zx} & m_{zy} & s_z \end{bmatrix} \]

where the scale-factor errors \(s\) and the six misalignments \(m\) are independent, zero-mean and normally distributed, with the spreads of the spec's scale_factor_ppm and misalignment_urad [dimensionless, rad].

docs.title: Dynamic bias: a first-order Gauss–Markov process
docs.text:
Each axis's dynamic bias \(b_d\) relaxes towards zero while being kicked by white noise:

\[ \dot b_d = -\frac{b_d}{\tau_c} + w_b, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[w_b(t)\,w_b(t')\right] = \frac{2\sigma^2}{\tau_c}\,\delta(t - t') \]

where \(\tau_c\) is the correlation time (bias_tau_s) [s] and \(\sigma\) the steady-state spread of the bias [rad/s or m/s²]. Its correlation with itself decays as \(e^{-|\Delta t|/\tau_c}\): over times much shorter than \(\tau_c\) it looks like a constant bias, over much longer times like noise.

A datasheet does not quote \(\sigma\). It quotes the bias instability \(B\), the floor of the sensor's Allan deviation, the standard measure of how much a sensor's average output varies between successive averaging windows of length \(T\). For white noise plus a Gauss–Markov bias:

\[ \sigma_A^2(T) = \frac{N^2}{T} + \frac{\sigma^2\tau_c^2}{T^2}\left(\frac{2T}{\tau_c} - 3 + 4e^{-T/\tau_c} - e^{-2T/\tau_c}\right) \]

where \(\sigma_A\) is the Allan deviation [rad/s or m/s²], \(T\) the averaging time [s] and \(N\) the white-noise density defined below. The Gauss–Markov term peaks at \(0.6174\,\sigma\) when \(T = 1.89\,\tau_c\). ins_sim therefore sets

\[ \sigma = \frac{B}{0.6174} \]

so the simulated Allan deviation peaks at exactly the datasheet value. See Validation for how to choose \(\tau_c\) from a datasheet's Allan plot.

docs.title: White noise
docs.text:
White noise of density \(N\) integrates into a random walk whose spread grows with the square root of time:

\[ \sigma_\theta(t) = N\sqrt{t} \]

where \(N\) is the ARW (gyro) [rad/√s] or VRW (accelerometer) [m/s/√s], and \(\sigma_\theta\) the spread of the integrated angle [rad] or velocity [m/s].

docs.title: Initial alignment
docs.text:
Before navigating, an INS aligns itself at rest. It levels by finding which way gravity points, which leaves a tilt error of about the accelerometer bias over \(g\). It finds North by gyrocompassing, measuring the direction of the Earth's rotation, which leaves a heading error of about the East-pointing gyro's bias over \(\omega_{ie}\cos L_b\). Each trial draws this residual alignment error as the initial attitude error:

\[ \delta\psivec{nb}{n}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\; \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_\text{tilt}^2,\ \sigma_\text{tilt}^2,\ \sigma_\text{heading}^2\right)\right) \]

For the packaged spec, 25 µg over \(g\) is 0.0014°, and 0.01 °/h over the Earth's horizontal rotation at 18.5° N is 0.04°: the spec's tilt and heading values.

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
1. Datasheet units to SI. The YAML spec is converted as it is loaded:

EquationCode Datasheet unit Factor to SI SI unit °/√h \(\pi/180/60\) rad/√s °/h \(\pi/180/3600\) rad/s µg \(9.80665 \times 10^{-6}\) m/s² m/s/√h \(1/60\) m/s/√s ppm, µrad \(10^{-6}\) –, rad 
DEG_HR = np.pi / 180 / 3600
return IMUSpec(
    gyro_arw     = g["arw_deg_per_rt_hr"]          * np.pi / 180 / 60,
    gyro_bias_instability = g["bias_instab_deg_per_hr"]  * DEG_HR,
    gyro_bias_tau         = g["bias_tau_s"],
    gyro_br_std  = g["repeatability_deg_per_hr"]   * DEG_HR,
    gyro_sf_std  = g.get("scale_factor_ppm", 0.0)   * 1e-6,
    gyro_ma_std  = g.get("misalignment_urad", 0.0)  * 1e-6,
    accel_vrw    = a["vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr"]      / 60,
    accel_bias_instability = a["bias_instab_ug"]     * 1e-6 * 9.80665,
    accel_bias_tau         = a["bias_tau_s"],
    accel_br_std = a["repeatability_ug"]            * 1e-6 * 9.80665,
    accel_sf_std = a.get("scale_factor_ppm", 0.0)   * 1e-6,
    accel_ma_std = a.get("misalignment_urad", 0.0)  * 1e-6,
    align_tilt_std    = al.get("tilt_std_deg", 0.0)    * np.pi / 180,
    align_heading_std = al.get("heading_std_deg", 0.0) * np.pi / 180,
    baro = None if baro is None else baro_spec_from_yaml(baro),
)

2. Scale factor and misalignment, drawn once per trial:

EquationCode \[ \mathbf{y}_\text{scaled} = \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{y} \]

where \(\mathbf{y}\) is the true angular rate or specific force.

# Per-run multiplicative errors (scale factor + misalignment). With
# zero stds these are exact identity transforms, preserving the
# zero-noise passthrough property.
M = _error_matrix(rng, sf_std, ma_std)
scaled = truth_triad @ (np.eye(3) + M).T          # (I + M)·truth

3. Static bias, drawn once per trial:

EquationCode \[ \mathbf{b}_s \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\ \sigma_\text{BR}^2\Ithree\right) \]

where \(\sigma_\text{BR}\) is the turn-on bias repeatability.

# Static (turn-on) bias, per axis, constant over the run
b_s = rng.normal(0.0, bs_std, size=3)

4. Dynamic bias. The exact discrete form of the Gauss–Markov process, started in its steady state:

EquationCode \[ b_{d,k+1} = a\,b_{d,k} + \sqrt{1 - a^2}\,\sigma\,u_{k+1}, \qquad a = e^{-\tau_i/\tau_c}, \qquad b_{d,0} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \]

where \(u_k\) are independent standard normal numbers. The variance is \(\sigma^2\) at every sample, whatever the sample interval.

# Dynamic (Gauss-Markov) bias: discrete AR(1) recursion
#   b_d[k+1] = a·b_d[k] + √(1−a²)·σ·u[k+1],   a = exp(−tau_i/τ),
# started in its stationary distribution, b_d[0] ~ N(0, σ²), so its
# variance is σ² from the first sample on.
b_d = gauss_markov(rng, n_samples, tau_i, bd_std, bd_tau)

The same process models the barometer's weather drift, so it lives in a shared helper:

# The IIR filter produces the zero-start response to u; the decaying
# initial state a^k·x[0] is added to it.
a = np.exp(-tau_i / tau_c)
s = np.sqrt(1.0 - a * a) * sigma
x0 = rng.normal(0.0, sigma, size=n_axes)
u = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_axes)); u[0] = 0.0
return (lfilter([1.0], [1.0, -a], s * u, axis=0)
        + a ** np.arange(n_samples)[:, None] * x0)

5. White noise. The per-sample spread that integrates to \(N\sqrt{t}\):

EquationCode \[ w_k \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0,\ \frac{N^2}{\tau_i}\right) \] 
# White noise: density/√tau_i is the discrete-time σ that makes the
# integrated angle (velocity) uncertainty grow as density·√t,
# independent of the sample rate.
w = rng.normal(0.0, noise_density / np.sqrt(tau_i), size=(n_samples, 3))

6. Initial alignment error, drawn once per trial:

EquationCode \[ \delta\psivec{nb}{n}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\; \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_\text{tilt}^2,\ \sigma_\text{tilt}^2,\ \sigma_\text{heading}^2\right)\right) \] 
return rng.normal(0.0, [spec.align_tilt_std,
                        spec.align_tilt_std,
                        spec.align_heading_std])

The gyro triad, the accelerometer triad and the alignment error each draw from their own random stream, and each triad draws its terms in a fixed order, whether or not their spreads are zero. Changing one error's spread therefore leaves every other error's realization unchanged, which makes comparisons between specs fair (see Monte Carlo evaluation).

Compared with Groves (2013)

The structure is Groves' sensor model1: a bias, a matrix of scale-factor and cross-coupling errors, and noise. Groves also includes a gyro bias proportional to specific force (the g-dependent bias) and output quantization; ins_sim models neither.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
The Allan deviation of a simulated stationary gyro with the packaged spec's noise. At short averaging times the white noise dominates, falling with a slope of −½. At long times the Gauss–Markov bias takes over and peaks at the datasheet bias instability, 0.01 °/h, at 1.89 hours. The Validation page checks this curve against the formula above, together with the angle random walk and the stationarity of the Gauss–Markov bias.

The example output below shows why the bias, not the noise, sets an INS's long-term performance. At 10 Hz each gyro sample's noise is 0.38 °/h, 38 times the bias instability, but it averages away; the bias does not.

docs.title: Assumptions & limitations
docs.text:
Assumptions & limitations

  • Not modelled: g-dependent gyro bias, quantization, rate random walk, scale-factor nonlinearity and asymmetry, temperature effects, and errors driven by vibration.
  • One Gauss–Markov hump. A real sensor's Allan deviation is often flat near its floor over a decade or more of averaging time. One Gauss–Markov process matches the datasheet value only at its peak, and falls below the real sensor on either side.
  • Independent alignment errors. A real INS aligns with its biases present, so the initial tilt largely cancels the accelerometer bias, and the initial heading error is tied to the East gyro's bias. ins_sim draws them independently, which is pessimistic early in a flight.
  • Constant parameters. The spreads do not change with temperature or time, and nothing estimates or corrects the errors during the run: there is no aiding apart from the barometer.

docs.text:

This example loads the packaged spec and prints its datasheet values next to the model parameters derived from them:

ScriptOutput 
"""The packaged IMU spec: datasheet values, and the model parameters derived from them."""

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_imu_spec_path
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import GM_ALLAN_PEAK, load_imu_spec

spec = load_imu_spec(str(default_imu_spec_path()))   # converted to SI on loading
tau_i = 0.1                                          # IMU output interval [s]
DEG_PER_HOUR = np.deg2rad(1.0) / 3600.0              # 1 °/h in rad/s
MICRO_G = 9.80665e-6                                 # 1 µg in m/s²


def show(label: str, value: float, unit: str) -> None:
    print(f"  {label:<42s}{value:9.4f} {unit}")


print("Gyro")
show("bias instability B (datasheet)", spec.gyro_bias_instability / DEG_PER_HOUR, "°/h")
show(f"Gauss-Markov spread, B / {GM_ALLAN_PEAK:.4f}", spec.gyro_gm_std / DEG_PER_HOUR, "°/h")
show("white noise per sample, ARW / sqrt(tau_i)", spec.gyro_arw / np.sqrt(tau_i) / DEG_PER_HOUR, "°/h")
print("Accelerometer")
show("bias instability B (datasheet)", spec.accel_bias_instability / MICRO_G, "µg")
show(f"Gauss-Markov spread, B / {GM_ALLAN_PEAK:.4f}", spec.accel_gm_std / MICRO_G, "µg")
show("white noise per sample, VRW / sqrt(tau_i)", spec.accel_vrw / np.sqrt(tau_i) / MICRO_G, "µg")
print("Initial alignment")
show("tilt spread", np.rad2deg(spec.align_tilt_std), "°")
show("heading spread", np.rad2deg(spec.align_heading_std), "°")

docs.title: Strapdown mechanization
docs.text:
The mechanization is the navigator itself: the equations that turn the gyro and accelerometer outputs back into attitude, velocity and position. It integrates the measured angular rate into attitude. It uses that attitude to resolve the measured specific force along North, East and Down, adds gravity back, and removes the apparent forces of the rotating Earth. It then integrates the result twice, into velocity and position. Every sensor error passes through these equations, and the INS error model follows from them. ins_sim implements the local-navigation-frame form of Groves1.

Key results

  • Each step performs four updates (attitude, specific-force resolution, velocity, position) after re-evaluating Earth rate, transport rate, gravity and the radii of curvature at the current state.
  • The attitude update applies the exact rotation-vector exponential of the body's rate relative to NED.
  • The basic velocity and position updates are first-order (forward Euler), on purpose: the default truth generator inverts exactly these steps.
  • The optional precision mechanization adds coning, rotation and sculling corrections and a trapezoidal position update, for the outputs of a real, integrating IMU. On the packaged mission at a 0.1 s step it cuts the navigator's own error from 1.7 km to about 2 m.

docs.title: Physical picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    G["Gyros<br/>ω̃<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>"] --> ATT["Attitude update<br/>C<sub>b</sub><sup>n</sup>"]
    A["Accelerometers<br/>f̃<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>"] --> RES["Resolve in NED<br/>f<sub>ib</sub><sup>n</sup> = C<sub>b</sub><sup>n</sup> f̃<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>"]
    ATT --> RES
    RES --> VEL["Velocity update<br/>+ gravity, − Coriolis"]
    VEL --> POS["Position update<br/>L<sub>b</sub>, λ<sub>b</sub>, h<sub>b</sub>"]
    EARTH(["Earth model<br/>ω<sub>ie</sub><sup>n</sup>, ω<sub>en</sub><sup>n</sup>, g, R<sub>N</sub>, R<sub>E</sub>"])
    POS -.-> EARTH
    VEL -.-> EARTH
    EARTH -.-> ATT
    EARTH -.-> VEL

The sensors are strapped to the vehicle, so they measure along the body axes. The navigator keeps track of the attitude and uses it to resolve each specific-force measurement in NED. What it measures is not acceleration, though. Specific force excludes gravity, which the navigator must add from its gravity model. It also includes the apparent accelerations of a rotating, curved frame, which the navigator must remove: the Coriolis term, and the transport term that keeps a vehicle following the curved Earth. The Earth model needs the current position and velocity, so every update feeds the next.

docs.title: Continuous-time model
docs.text:
In the local navigation frame, the navigation equations are:

\[ \Cmat[\dot]{b}{n} = \Cmat{b}{n}\Wmat{ib}{b} - \left(\Wmat{ie}{n} + \Wmat{en}{n}\right)\Cmat{b}{n} \] \[ \vvec[\dot]{eb}{n} = \Cmat{b}{n}\fvec{ib}{b} + \gvec{b}{n} - \left(\Wmat{en}{n} + 2\,\Wmat{ie}{n}\right)\vvec{eb}{n} \] \[ \dot L_b = \frac{v_N}{R_N + h_b}, \qquad \dot\lambda_b = \frac{v_E}{(R_E + h_b)\cos L_b}, \qquad \dot h_b = -v_D \]

where:

  • \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) is the attitude, and \(\vvec{eb}{n} = (v_N, v_E, v_D)\) the velocity relative to the Earth, resolved in NED [m/s];
  • \(\Wmat{ib}{b}\) and \(\fvec{ib}{b}\) hold the gyro and accelerometer outputs [rad/s, m/s²];
  • \(\Wmat{ie}{n}\) and \(\Wmat{en}{n}\) are the skew-symmetric matrices of Earth rate and transport rate [rad/s];
  • \(\gvec{b}{n}\) is gravity [m/s²], and \(L_b\), \(\lambda_b\), \(h_b\), \(R_N\), \(R_E\) are as on Earth & gravity.

The attitude equation is explained on Frames & attitude. In the velocity equation, \(2\Wmat{ie}{n}\vvec{eb}{n}\) is the Coriolis acceleration of a body moving over the rotating Earth, and \(\Wmat{en}{n}\vvec{eb}{n}\) the acceleration needed to follow the Earth's curvature. A vehicle at rest senses only the Earth's rotation and the reaction to gravity, and every derivative is then zero.

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
Each step takes the state at sample \(k\) to sample \(k+1\), one IMU interval \(\tau_i\) later. A tilde marks the sensor outputs; every other quantity is the navigator's own.

1. Frame rates and gravity at the current state:

EquationCode \[ \wvec{in}{n} = \wvec{ie}{n}(L_{b,k}) + \wvec{en}{n}(\vvec{eb}{n}(k), L_{b,k}, h_{b,k}), \qquad \gvec{b}{n} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & g(L_{b,k}, h_{b,k}) \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T} \] 
# --- 1. Local rotating-Earth quantities at step k --------------
omega_ie_n = earth_rate_n(L_b[k])
omega_en_n = transport_rate_n(v_eb_n[k], L_b[k], h_b[k])
omega_in_n = omega_ie_n + omega_en_n                   # nav-frame rate
g_b_n[2] = normal_gravity(L_b[k], h_b[k])

2. Body rate relative to NED. Remove the NED frame's own rotation, resolved in body axes, from what the gyros measured:

EquationCode \[ \wvec{nb}{b} = \wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} - \Cmat{n}{b}\,\wvec{in}{n} \] 
# --- 2. Body rate relative to the nav frame ------------------
# The gyro saw omega_ib^b. Subtract the nav frame's own rotation
# (resolved in body axes) to get what drives the b→n attitude update.
C_n_b = C_b_n.inv()
omega_nb_b = meas_omega_ib_b[k] - C_n_b.apply(omega_in_n)

3. Attitude update. Rotate the attitude by the body's rotation over the step, as an exact rotation vector:

EquationCode \[ \Cmat{b}{n}(k+1) = \Cmat{b}{n}(k)\,\exp\left(\skew{\wvec{nb}{b}\,\tau_i}\right) \]

This is the exact solution of the attitude equation when \(\wvec{nb}{b}\) is constant over the step.

# --- 3. Attitude update (exact rotation-vector exponential) ---
dC = Rot.from_rotvec(omega_nb_b * tau_i)
C_b_n_next = C_b_n * dC                                # right-mult: body increment
q_b_n[k+1] = C_b_n_next.as_quat() # pyright: ignore[reportCallIssue]

4. Specific force in NED, with the attitude at the start of the step:

EquationCode \[ \fvec{ib}{n} = \Cmat{b}{n}(k)\,\fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} \] 
# --- 4. Specific force in NED (forward Euler — consistent with
#        the truth IMU, which uses the same first-order scheme) ---
f_ib_n = C_b_n.apply(meas_f_ib_b[k])

5. Velocity update, forward Euler. The code also holds the barometric damping terms, explained on Vertical channel:

EquationCode \[ \vvec{eb}{n}(k+1) = \vvec{eb}{n}(k) + \left[\fvec{ib}{n} - \left(2\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right)\times\vvec{eb}{n}(k) + \gvec{b}{n}\right]\tau_i \] 
# --- 5. Rotating-frame velocity update ------------------------
coriolis = np.cross(2.0 * omega_ie_n + omega_en_n, v_eb_n[k])
v_eb_n_dot = f_ib_n - coriolis + g_b_n
# Baro damping: the height residual corrects vertical velocity
# (K2) and updates the accel-error integrator (K3); a positive
# residual (INS high) commands positive Down velocity.
if meas_h_b is not None:
    baro_residual = h_b[k] - meas_h_b[k]
    v_eb_n_dot[2] += K2 * baro_residual + acc_corr
    acc_corr += K3 * baro_residual * tau_i
v_eb_n[k+1] = v_eb_n[k] + v_eb_n_dot * tau_i

6. Position update, forward Euler, with the radii of curvature at the start of the step:

EquationCode \[ L_{b,k+1} = L_{b,k} + \frac{v_{N,k}\,\tau_i}{R_N + h_{b,k}}, \quad \lambda_{b,k+1} = \lambda_{b,k} + \frac{v_{E,k}\,\tau_i}{(R_E + h_{b,k})\cos L_{b,k}}, \quad h_{b,k+1} = h_{b,k} - v_{D,k}\,\tau_i \] 
# --- 6. Curvilinear position (forward Euler — matches truth) --
R_N, R_E = wgs84_radii(L_b[k])
L_b[k+1] = L_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k][0] / (R_N + h_b[k])) * tau_i
lambda_b[k+1] = lambda_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k][1] /
                               ((R_E + h_b[k]) * np.cos(L_b[k]))) * tau_i
h_b[k+1] = h_b[k] - v_eb_n[k][2] * tau_i
if meas_h_b is not None:
    h_b[k+1] -= K1 * baro_residual * tau_i

Finally, the new position is also converted to metres from the start point, \(\rvec{lb}{l}\), for drawing tracks (see Frames & attitude).

Compared with Groves (2013)

This is Groves' local-navigation-frame mechanization1, with three deliberate differences:

  • Attitude. Groves' basic attitude update is the first-order truncation \(\Cmat{b}{n}(\Ithree + \Wmat{ib}{b}\tau_i) - \Wmat{in}{n}\Cmat{b}{n}\tau_i\). ins_sim applies the exact exponential of the same rotation, which agrees with it to first order and keeps the attitude a pure rotation.
  • Position. Groves averages the velocities at the start and end of the step; ins_sim uses the velocity at the start.
  • Precision corrections are optional. Groves' precision mechanization corrects for the body turning within each step. ins_sim offers it as a separate mode.

The first-order choices keep the navigator the exact inverse of the default truth generator.

docs.title: Precision mechanization
docs.text:
A real IMU does not sample the angular rate and specific force at an instant. It integrates them over each interval and reports the increments: the attitude increment \(\avec{ib}{b} = \int \wvec{ib}{b}\,dt\) and the velocity increment \(\uvec{ib}{b} = \int \fvec{ib}{b}\,dt\), both in body axes. The basic update treats them as rates held constant over the step, and that misses three effects of the body turning while the IMU integrates:

  • Rotation. The specific force is integrated in body axes that keep turning, so resolving the whole increment with the start attitude is wrong by about \(\tfrac12\,\avec{ib}{b}\times\uvec{ib}{b}\). In a turn at rate \(\dot\psi\) and speed \(v\) this is a velocity error along the flight path that grows at \(\tfrac12 v\dot\psi^2\tau_i\), 0.03 m/s² for an airliner's 3 °/s turn at a 0.1 s step.
  • Coning. When the rotation axis itself moves within the step, the rotation is not \(\avec{ib}{b}\): rotations do not commute. A vibration that cones the IMU drifts the attitude even though no gyro has a bias.
  • Sculling. When a rotation oscillates in phase with a specific force along another axis, the true velocity increment differs from \(\uvec{ib}{b}\) in a way that does not average out.

ins_sim's precision mechanization corrects all three with Savage's one-sample-plus-previous algorithms2, which estimate how the rates change within the step from the previous step's increments. It also updates the position with the velocities at both ends of the step. The steps below replace steps 2 to 6; step 1 is unchanged.

P1. Midpoint rates. The nav-frame rate, gravity and Coriolis term are needed over the whole step, so each is extrapolated to its middle from this step and the previous one:

EquationCode \[ \bar{\mathbf{x}} = \tfrac32\,\mathbf{x}_k - \tfrac12\,\mathbf{x}_{k-1}, \qquad \mathbf{x} \in \left\{\wvec{in}{n},\ \gvec{b}{n} - \left(2\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right)\times\vvec{eb}{n}\right\} \] 
# The nav-frame rate, gravity and Coriolis at the middle of the
# interval, extrapolated from this step and the previous one.
gravity_coriolis = g_b_n - _cross(2.0 * omega_ie_n + omega_en_n, v_eb_n[k])
if k == 0:
    omega_in_prev, gravity_coriolis_prev = omega_in_n, gravity_coriolis
omega_in_mid = 1.5 * omega_in_n - 0.5 * omega_in_prev
gravity_coriolis_mid = 1.5 * gravity_coriolis - 0.5 * gravity_coriolis_prev
omega_in_prev, gravity_coriolis_prev = omega_in_n, gravity_coriolis

P2. Attitude, with the coning correction on the body side and the nav frame's rotation over the step on the other:

EquationCode \[ \boldsymbol{\phi}_k = \avec{ib,k}{b} + \tfrac{1}{12}\,\avec{ib,k-1}{b}\times\avec{ib,k}{b}, \qquad \Cmat{b}{n}(k+1) = \exp\left(-\skew{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}\right)\Cmat{b}{n}(k)\exp\left(\skew{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}\right), \qquad \boldsymbol{\zeta} = \wvec[\bar]{in}{n}\,\tau_i \] 
return alpha + _cross(alpha_prev, alpha) / 12.0

alpha = meas_omega_ib_b[k] * tau_i                 # alpha_ib^b
upsilon = meas_f_ib_b[k] * tau_i                   # upsilon_ib^b
zeta = omega_in_mid * tau_i                        # nav-frame rotation
phi = coning_correction(alpha_prev, alpha)
C_b_n_next = Rot.from_rotvec(-zeta) * C_b_n * Rot.from_rotvec(phi)

P3. Velocity. The rotation and sculling corrections give the velocity increment in the body axes at the start of the step, which is resolved in NED and corrected for half the nav frame's rotation:

EquationCode \[ \Delta\mathbf{v}^{b} = \uvec{ib,k}{b} + \tfrac12\,\avec{ib,k}{b}\times\uvec{ib,k}{b} + \tfrac{1}{12}\left(\avec{ib,k-1}{b}\times\uvec{ib,k}{b} + \uvec{ib,k-1}{b}\times\avec{ib,k}{b}\right) \] \[ \vvec{eb}{n}(k+1) = \vvec{eb}{n}(k) + \Cmat{b}{n}(k)\,\Delta\mathbf{v}^{b} - \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol{\zeta}\times\Cmat{b}{n}(k)\,\uvec{ib,k}{b} + \overline{\gvec{b}{n} - \left(2\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right)\times\vvec{eb}{n}}\;\tau_i \]

where the overlined term is the midpoint value from P1.

rotation = 0.5 * _cross(alpha, upsilon)
sculling = (_cross(alpha_prev, upsilon) + _cross(upsilon_prev, alpha)) / 12.0
return upsilon + rotation + sculling

dv_b = sculling_correction(alpha_prev, upsilon_prev, alpha, upsilon)
dv_sf_n = C_b_n.apply(dv_b) - 0.5 * _cross(zeta, C_b_n.apply(upsilon))
v_eb_n[k+1] = v_eb_n[k] + dv_sf_n + gravity_coriolis_mid * tau_i

P4. Position, by the trapezoidal rule:

EquationCode \[ h_{b,k+1} = h_{b,k} - \tfrac12\left(v_{D,k} + v_{D,k+1}\right)\tau_i, \qquad L_{b,k+1} = L_{b,k} + \tfrac12\left(\frac{v_{N,k}}{R_{N,k} + h_{b,k}} + \frac{v_{N,k+1}}{R_{N,k+1} + h_{b,k+1}}\right)\tau_i \]

and likewise for \(\lambda_b\), with \(R_E\) and \(\cos L_b\) at each end. The radii at the end of the step are taken at a latitude predicted with the start values, which keeps the update second order.

R_N, R_E = wgs84_radii(L_b[k])
h_b[k+1] = h_b[k] - 0.5 * (v_eb_n[k, 2] + v_eb_n[k+1, 2]) * tau_i
L_pred = L_b[k] + v_eb_n[k, 0] / (R_N + h_b[k]) * tau_i
R_N_next, R_E_next = wgs84_radii(L_pred)
L_b[k+1] = L_b[k] + 0.5 * (v_eb_n[k, 0] / (R_N + h_b[k])
                           + v_eb_n[k+1, 0] / (R_N_next + h_b[k+1])) * tau_i
lambda_b[k+1] = lambda_b[k] + 0.5 * (
    v_eb_n[k, 1] / ((R_E + h_b[k]) * np.cos(L_b[k]))
    + v_eb_n[k+1, 1] / ((R_E_next + h_b[k+1]) * np.cos(L_b[k+1]))) * tau_i

At the first step there is no previous step: the corrections that need one are left out, and the midpoint rates are the start values.

Pair the precision mechanization with an integrating IMU

The default truth's outputs are the exact inverse of the basic update, so the basic mechanization reproduces that truth exactly and the precision corrections would only add an error. They pay off on the outputs of an integrating IMU, which ins_sim generates when the truth is oversampled: set oversample in build_trajectory, --oversample on the command line, or Truth oversampling under Advanced in the app. The GUI and the command line print a note when the precision mechanization runs without it.

On an integrating IMU, the basic mechanization's error is first order in \(\tau_i\): it halves when the step halves. The precision mechanization's falls at least four times as fast. The Validation page checks each correction against the classical coning and sculling motions, and compares the two mechanizations on the packaged mission.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
The navigator, fed the ideal outputs of the packaged mission's truth, reproduces the truth to within \(2.3 \times 10^{-8}\) m over the whole 80 minutes. The difference is floating-point rounding, which accumulates in small steps. This is the zero-noise round trip of the Validation page. It proves that the navigator and the truth generator are consistent. It cannot show how accurately the navigator integrates continuous motion, because the truth is built from the navigator's own discrete steps.

The example below runs the navigator on a level IMU at rest at 45° N. With perfect sensors it stays exactly at rest: the gyros' Earth rate is removed by step 2, and the accelerometers' reaction to gravity is cancelled by step 5. A 0.01 °/h gyro bias moves it 1.3 km in an hour.

docs.title: Assumptions & limitations
docs.text:
Assumptions & limitations

  • First-order basic update. The basic velocity and position updates are forward Euler, the specific force is resolved with the attitude at the start of each step, and there are no coning or sculling corrections. Against the default truth these errors are invisible, because the truth inverts them exactly (see Truth trajectory & ideal IMU). An oversampled truth exposes them, and the precision mechanization removes most of them.
  • Precision update to second order. The precision mechanization's remaining error falls with the square of the step or faster. Its corrections assume the rates change smoothly over two steps, so a manoeuvre much shorter than that, such as a 6 °/s roll-in sampled at 1 s, still leaves an error.
  • Known start. Each run starts from the true position and velocity. Only the attitude starts in error, by the drawn alignment error; the alignment itself is not simulated.
  • Vertical channel. Without a height reference the vertical channel diverges. By default a barometric loop holds it (see Vertical channel).
  • No aiding. Apart from the barometer, nothing corrects the navigator: there is no GNSS or other measurement update.
  • Not over the poles, where the NED frame is undefined.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text:
Quantity Equation Implemented in The whole mechanization Steps 1 to 6, or 1 and P1 to P4 with mechanization="precision" strapdown_navgrade Coning correction \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_k\) coning_correction Rotation and sculling corrections \(\Delta\mathbf{v}^{b}\) sculling_correction Initial state \(L_b\), \(\lambda_b\), \(h_b\), \(\vvec{eb}{n}\), \(\qvec{b}{n}\) NavState Output history Every state, plus \(\rvec{lb}{l}\) NavSolution Earth rate, transport rate, gravity, radii Step 1 earth_rate_n, transport_rate_n, normal_gravity, wgs84_radii

This example runs the navigator for an hour on a level IMU at rest at 45° N, first with perfect sensors and then with a 0.01 °/h bias on the gyro that points East:

ScriptOutput 
"""The navigator on a level IMU at rest at 45° N: perfect sensors, then a gyro bias."""

import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

from ins_sim.core.earth_model import earth_rate_n, normal_gravity
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.navigation.strapdown import NavState, strapdown_navgrade

L_b, tau_i, M = np.deg2rad(45.0), 1.0, 3601          # one hour at 1 s
baro = np.zeros(M)                                    # an ideal barometer: h_b = 0

# At rest, a perfect IMU senses Earth rate and the reaction to gravity.
omega_ib_b = np.tile(earth_rate_n(L_b), (M, 1))
f_ib_b = np.tile([0.0, 0.0, -normal_gravity(L_b, 0.0)], (M, 1))
start = NavState(L_b, 0.0, 0.0, np.zeros(3), Rotation.identity().as_quat())

nav = strapdown_navgrade(omega_ib_b, f_ib_b, start, tau_i, meas_h_b=baro)
print(f"Perfect sensors: largest speed in 1 h = {np.abs(nav.v_eb_n).max():.1f} m/s")

# The same, with a 0.01 °/h bias on the gyro that points East (body y).
b_g = np.deg2rad(0.01) / 3600.0
nav = strapdown_navgrade(omega_ib_b + [0.0, b_g, 0.0], f_ib_b, start, tau_i, meas_h_b=baro)
delta_r_eb_n = position_error(nav.L_b, nav.lambda_b, nav.h_b, L_b, 0.0, 0.0)
print(f"0.01 °/h gyro bias: horizontal error after 1 h = "
      f"{np.hypot(*delta_r_eb_n[-1, :2]):.0f} m")

Perfect sensors: largest speed in 1 h = 0.0 m/s
0.01 °/h gyro bias: horizontal error after 1 h = 1346 m

The 1.3 km is close to the single-channel prediction for a gyro bias, \(R\,b_g\,(t - \sin\omega_s t/\omega_s)\) = 1.35 km after an hour (see INS error model).

This example runs both mechanizations on the packaged mission at 1 s steps with perfect sensors, first on the default truth and then on an integrating IMU's outputs:

ScriptOutput 
"""Both mechanizations on an integrating IMU's outputs, with perfect sensors."""

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_trajectory_path
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.navigation.strapdown import NavState, strapdown_navgrade
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

for oversample in (None, 10):
    # The packaged mission at 1 s steps; oversampled, the IMU outputs are
    # averages over each step of a mission built ten times as finely.
    truth = build_trajectory(str(default_trajectory_path()), tau_i=1.0,
                             oversample=oversample).truth
    start = NavState(truth.L_b[0], truth.lambda_b[0], truth.h_b[0],
                     truth.v_eb_n[0], truth.C_b_n[0].as_quat())
    print(f"Truth oversampling: {oversample or 'off'}")
    for mechanization in ("basic", "precision"):
        nav = strapdown_navgrade(truth.omega_ib_b, truth.f_ib_b, start, truth.tau_i,
                                 meas_h_b=truth.h_b, mechanization=mechanization)
        delta_r_eb_n = position_error(nav.L_b, nav.lambda_b, nav.h_b,
                                      truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)
        largest = np.hypot(delta_r_eb_n[:, 0], delta_r_eb_n[:, 1]).max()
        print(f"  {mechanization:9s}  largest horizontal error {largest:7.0f} m")

Truth oversampling: off
  basic      largest horizontal error       0 m
  precision  largest horizontal error   20321 m
Truth oversampling: 10
  basic      largest horizontal error   19936 m
  precision  largest horizontal error     198 m

Each mechanization is exact on the outputs it was built for and about 20 km off on the other's. On the integrating IMU the precision update is 100 times closer; the 198 m it keeps comes from the roll into each turn, which at 6 °/s is fast for a 1 s step. At the app's 0.1 s it is about 2 m.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Groves (2013), Chapter 5, for the inertial navigation equations in the local navigation frame, and their precision versions. ↩↩

  2. Savage (1998a) and Savage (1998b) derive the coning and sculling algorithms, including the one-sample-plus-previous forms used here. Groves (2013), Chapter 5, presents them within the precision navigation equations. ↩

docs.title: Monte Carlo evaluation
docs.text:
One simulated flight shows one possible outcome of one set of sensor errors. To say how good a navigator is, you need the spread of outcomes over all the errors its IMU might have. ins_sim estimates that spread empirically: it flies the same truth trajectory many times, each time with an independent draw of every sensor and alignment error, and summarizes the ensemble with statistics such as ±3σ bands and the CEP. Every results tab in the GUI is such a summary, and the GUI's Monte Carlo iterations setting is the number of trials.

Key results

  • Each trial flies the same truth with an independent draw of the initial alignment error and of every gyro and accelerometer error, through the full nonlinear navigator.
  • Errors are the estimate minus the truth, resolved in NED at the true position.
  • At every sample the trials are summarized as a mean with ±3σ bands, the CEP (the median horizontal error) and the 95th percentile.
  • With \(N\) trials, an estimated σ is uncertain by about \(1/\sqrt{2(N - 1)}\): 10% for 50 trials.

docs.title: Physical picture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    SEED["Seed"] --> T1["Trial 1"]
    SEED --> T2["Trial 2"]
    SEED --> TN["Trial N"]
    T1 --> AL["Alignment error"]
    T1 --> IMU["IMU errors"]
    IMU --> GY["Gyro triad"]
    IMU --> AC["Accelerometer triad"]

The navigation error of an INS is random: it depends on the particular biases, noise and alignment error of a particular run. Running many trials turns that randomness into a distribution. The spread of that distribution at each moment is the simulator's measure of performance, and how it grows with time is the IMU's signature.

Each trial gets its own random stream, split again for each error source. Every number a trial draws therefore depends only on the seed and on which trial and source it belongs to.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Each trial's errors are formed exactly as defined on Notation & conventions: the attitude error \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\) (North tilt, East tilt, heading), the velocity error \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n}\), and the position error \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\) in metres along North, East and Down at the true position.

docs.title: Mean and ±3σ bands
docs.text:
For any error component \(x\), with \(x_i(t)\) its value in trial \(i\):

\[ \bar x(t) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i(t), \qquad s(t) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(x_i(t) - \bar x(t)\right)^2} \]

where \(N\) is the number of trials, \(\bar x\) the ensemble mean and \(s\) the sample standard deviation. The Attitude Errors, Velocity Errors and Position Errors tabs draw \(\bar x\) and the band \(\bar x \pm 3s\). For a normally distributed error the band holds 99.7% of trials. Together, the three components' spreads are the diagonal of the empirical covariance

\[ \mathbf{P}(t) = \frac{1}{N - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\mathbf{x}_i(t) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}(t)\right) \left(\mathbf{x}_i(t) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}(t)\right)^{\mathsf T} \]

docs.title: CEP and percentiles
docs.text:
The horizontal radial error of trial \(i\) is \(\rho_i(t) = \sqrt{\delta r_{N,i}^2 + \delta r_{E,i}^2}\). Its median across trials is the circular error probable:

\[ \mathrm{CEP}(t) = \operatorname{median}_i\,\rho_i(t) \]

Half of the trials lie inside a circle of that radius. The CEP tab fits a straight line to the CEP over the first hour; its slope, in nautical miles per hour, is the usual one-number figure of merit for an INS. The 95th percentile of the 3-D error \(|\delta\rvec{eb}{n}|\) draws the error tube of the 3D Trajectory tab, and that of the horizontal error the envelope on the Map.

For a circular normal distribution with spread \(\sigma\) on each axis, \(\mathrm{CEP} = \sigma\sqrt{2\ln 2} \approx 1.18\,\sigma\). ins_sim takes the median of the trials instead, which assumes nothing about the distribution.

docs.title: Sampling uncertainty
docs.text:
Statistics from \(N\) trials are estimates. The relative uncertainty of an estimated standard deviation is about \(1/\sqrt{2(N - 1)}\):

Trials \(N\) 10 20 50 100 200 Uncertainty of \(s\) 24% 16% 10% 7% 5%

Tails converge more slowly than the middle. With 50 trials the 95th percentile rests on the two or three largest errors, so the error tube settles only with more trials than the CEP needs.

docs.title: Random streams
docs.text:
The random numbers come from a tree of independent streams, spawned from the seed: one per trial, then one per error source within the trial (the alignment error, the gyro triad, the accelerometer triad). Each triad draws its error terms in a fixed order (see IMU error model). Two properties follow:

  • A trial's errors do not depend on how many trials run: trial 7 is the same whether you run 10 trials or 100.
  • Changing one error source leaves every other source's realization unchanged. Two runs with the same seed and specs that differ only in, say, the accelerometer bias therefore differ only because of that bias. These common random numbers make comparisons sharp with few trials.

The GUI and the command-line tool both use the seed 42, so the same settings always give the same results.

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
1. One trial. Draw the alignment error, start the navigator from the truth with that attitude error, generate the noisy IMU outputs and navigate:

EquationCode \[ \Cmat[\hat]{b}{n}(0) = \exp\left(\skew{\delta\psivec{nb}{n}(0)}\right)\Cmat{b}{n}(0), \qquad \left(\wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}, \fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\right) = \text{IMU}\left(\wvec{ib}{b}, \fvec{ib}{b}\right) \] 
trial_rngs = np.random.default_rng(seed).spawn(n_trials)
C_b_n0 = truth.C_b_n[0]

n_done = n_trials
for i, trial_rng in enumerate(trial_rngs):
    if should_stop is not None and should_stop():
        n_done = i
        break
    rng_alignment, rng_imu, rng_baro = trial_rng.spawn(3)
    # Per-trial initial-alignment error delta_psi_nb^n: small NED tilts
    # plus an azimuth error, applied to the truth attitude (zero-mean
    # draws; exact truth initialization when the alignment stds are 0).
    delta_psi_nb_n0 = draw_initial_misalignment(spec, rng_alignment)
    est_C_b_n0 = Rot.from_rotvec(delta_psi_nb_n0) * C_b_n0
    init_state = NavState(
        truth.L_b[0], truth.lambda_b[0], truth.h_b[0],
        truth.v_eb_n[0].copy(),
        est_C_b_n0.as_quat(), # pyright: ignore[reportCallIssue]
    )
    meas_omega_ib_b, meas_f_ib_b = generate_imu_samples(truth, spec, rng_imu)
    if not baro_aiding:
        meas_h_b = None                                  # free-inertial
    elif spec.baro is None:
        meas_h_b = truth.h_b                             # ideal barometer
    else:
        meas_h_b = generate_baro_samples(truth, spec.baro, rng_baro)
    nav = strapdown_navgrade(
        meas_omega_ib_b, meas_f_ib_b, init_state, truth.tau_i,
        meas_h_b=meas_h_b, mechanization=mechanization)

2. Position error in metres, at the true position:

EquationCode \[ \delta\rvec{eb}{n} = \begin{bmatrix} (R_N + h_b)\,\delta L_b \\ (R_E + h_b)\cos L_b\,\delta\lambda_b \\ -\delta h_b \end{bmatrix} \] 
return np.stack([
    (R_N + h_b) * delta_L_b,
    (R_E + h_b) * np.cos(L_b) * delta_lambda_b,
    -delta_h_b,
], axis=-1)

3. Mean and spread for the bands:

EquationCode \[ \bar x(t) \pm 3\,s(t) \] 
mean = err_runs.mean(axis=0)
# Unbiased (N−1) spread; a single trial has no spread to estimate.
sigma = err_runs.std(axis=0, ddof=1 if len(err_runs) > 1 else 0)

4. CEP and its growth rate. The horizontal errors are in nautical miles and the time in hours:

EquationCode \[ \mathrm{CEP}(t) = \operatorname{median}_i\,\rho_i(t), \qquad \text{rate} = \text{slope of the least-squares line through } \mathrm{CEP}(t),\ t \le 1~\text{h} \] 
cep = np.percentile(horiz_err_nm, 50, axis=0)
mask = t_hr <= 1.0
if mask.sum() >= 2:
    coeffs = np.polyfit(t_hr[mask], cep[mask], 1)

5. Percentile envelope of the 3-D error:

EquationCode \[ r_{95}(t) = \text{95th percentile over the trials of } \left|\delta\rvec{eb}{n}(t)\right| \] 
return np.percentile(np.linalg.norm(delta_r_eb_n, axis=2), q, axis=0)

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
The Position Errors tab for 50 trials of the packaged mission with the navigation-grade spec. The mean error stays near zero, because every error source is zero-mean across trials, while the ±3σ bands grow to about 10 km North and 5 km East by the end of the 80-minute mission. The Down band levels off at about ±250 m once the climb ends: it is the barometer's own error, which the barometric loop passes into the height.

The CEP tab for the same run: every trial's horizontal error, and the straight-line fit to the CEP over the first hour, 1.3 nmi/h. That is close to what the gyro biases alone predict: the turn-on and in-run biases add up to about 0.02 °/h per axis, and each 0.01 °/h gives 0.6 nmi/h (see INS error model).

docs.title: Assumptions & limitations
docs.text:
Assumptions & limitations

  • Costly and noisy. Every statistic comes from nonlinear trials, so it costs \(N\) full simulations, and it is only as accurate as \(N\) allows. The covariance analysis predicts the same spreads in one pass, without sampling noise, as long as the errors stay small; the app draws its prediction as dashed lines.
  • Sampling error. Bands from a few trials are noisy, and tails need more trials than medians; see the table above.
  • One trajectory. Every trial flies the same truth trajectory. Only the sensor and alignment errors vary.
  • Only the modelled errors. A trial contains only the error sources on the IMU error model page, and the barometer's on the Vertical channel page.
  • Normality is not assumed, but the bands read best with it. The ±3σ bands hold 99.7% of trials only if the errors are normally distributed. The CEP and percentiles make no such assumption.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text:
Quantity Equation Implemented in The trials One trial per stream run_monte_carlo, MonteCarloResult Errors \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\), \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n}\), \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\) attitude_error, velocity_error, position_error Percentile envelope \(r_{95}(t)\) percentile_envelope Bands and CEP \(\bar x \pm 3s\), \(\mathrm{CEP}(t)\) _bands_figure and figure_cep in ins_sim/gui/figures.py

This example runs 25 trials of a short flight and summarizes them the way the GUI does: mean and 3σ for each axis, the CEP and the 95th percentile. Its exact numbers depend on the random draws, so this page does not show them:

"""A small Monte Carlo run, summarized the way the GUI summarizes it."""

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_imu_spec_path
from ins_sim.evaluation.errors import position_error
from ins_sim.evaluation.monte_carlo import percentile_envelope, run_monte_carlo
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import load_imu_spec
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import TruthTrajectory
from ins_sim.trajectory.spline import NEDSplinePath

# About 11 minutes at 150 m/s: 60 km north, then a gentle turn to the north-east.
path = NEDSplinePath([[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [60e3, 0.0, 0.0], [90e3, 30e3, 0.0]])
truth = TruthTrajectory.from_spline(path, speed=150.0, tau_i=2.0)
spec = load_imu_spec(str(default_imu_spec_path()))

mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=25, seed=42)
delta_r_eb_n = position_error(mc.est_L_b, mc.est_lambda_b, mc.est_h_b,
                              truth.L_b, truth.lambda_b, truth.h_b)

n_trials = len(delta_r_eb_n)
final = delta_r_eb_n[:, -1, :]                       # every trial's error at the end
mean, sigma = final.mean(axis=0), final.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
print(f"{n_trials} trials, {truth.t[-1] / 60:.0f} min of flight. At the end:")
for axis, name in enumerate(("North", "East", "Down")):
    print(f"  {name:5s} error: mean {mean[axis]:7.1f} m, 3-sigma {3.0 * sigma[axis]:6.1f} m")
print(f"  (each sigma is uncertain by about {100 / np.sqrt(2 * (n_trials - 1)):.0f}% "
      f"with {n_trials} trials)")
horizontal = np.linalg.norm(final[:, :2], axis=1)
print(f"  CEP, the median horizontal error: {np.median(horizontal):.1f} m")
print(f"  95th percentile of the 3-D error: {percentile_envelope(delta_r_eb_n, q=95)[-1]:.1f} m")

docs.title: Notation & conventions
docs.text:
Inertial navigation keeps track of several reference frames at once: the spinning Earth, the local North-East-Down directions, and the vehicle's own axes. Most confusion in INS mathematics comes from losing track of which frame a quantity describes, relative to what, and along which axes its components are written. These docs use the notation of Groves (2013), which writes all three facts into every symbol.

This page is the reference for every symbol used elsewhere in the docs. Each symbol has one meaning on every page. From v0.3.0 the Python code uses the same scheme, so an equation and the line of code that implements it share their names.

Key points

  • A kinematic symbol reads "motion of the object frame, relative to the reference frame, resolved in the axes frame": \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) is the angular rate of the body (b) relative to inertial space (i), expressed along the body axes (b).
  • \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) transforms a vector's components from body axes to North-East-Down axes.
  • A tilde marks a sensor measurement and a hat marks an estimate. Errors are always estimate minus truth.
  • Everything inside the simulator is in SI units.

docs.title: Reading a Groves symbol
docs.text:
Every kinematic vector carries three frame labels:

\[ \huge \boldsymbol{\omega}_{\textcolor[RGB]{232,89,12}{i}\,\textcolor[RGB]{28,126,214}{b}}^{\textcolor[RGB]{47,158,68}{b}} \] Slot In \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) Meaning Main symbol \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) The quantity: here, angular rate. First subscript i The reference frame the motion is measured relative to. Here: inertial space. Second subscript b The object frame whose motion is described. Here: the vehicle body. Superscript b The resolving axes: the frame whose axes the three components are written along. Here: the body axes.

The resolving axes can change without changing the physical quantity. The same velocity vector, resolved in two different frames, is related by a transformation matrix:

\[ \vvec{eb}{n} = \Cmat{b}{n}\,\vvec{eb}{b} \]

Three symbols are worth reading aloud, because they are what the sensors measure and what the navigator outputs:

  • \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) is what a gyro triad measures: the body's rotation rate relative to inertial space, along the sensor axes.
  • \(\fvec{ib}{b}\) is what an accelerometer triad measures: specific force (acceleration relative to inertial space, minus gravitation), along the sensor axes.
  • \(\vvec{eb}{n}\) is the ground velocity the navigator reports: the body's velocity relative to the Earth, in North, East and Down components.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text: Frame Label Origin Axes Role in ins_sim Earth-centred inertial (ECI) i Earth's centre Fixed relative to the distant stars The frame gyros and accelerometers measure motion against. Earth-centred, Earth-fixed (ECEF) e Earth's centre Rotate with the Earth at \(\omega_{ie}\) Velocity is Earth-referenced. Local navigation (NED) n The vehicle North, East, Down at the current position Attitude and velocity are resolved here. Body b The IMU x forward, y right, z down The sensor axes. Local tangent plane l The start point North, East, Down at the start point Drawing tracks relative to the start.

docs.title: Transformation matrices
docs.text:
\(\Cmat{\beta}{\alpha}\) transforms a vector's components from the \(\beta\)-frame axes to the \(\alpha\)-frame axes. These matrices are orthonormal, so the inverse transformation is the transpose:

\[ \Cmat{n}{b} = \left(\Cmat{b}{n}\right)^{\mathsf T} \]

docs.title: Skew-symmetric matrices
docs.text:
The cross product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) can be written as a matrix product, \(\skew{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b}\), with

\[ \skew{\mathbf{a}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The upper-case Greek symbol denotes the skew-symmetric form of an angular rate, e.g. \(\Wmat{ie}{n} = \skew{\wvec{ie}{n}}\).

docs.title: Decorations
docs.text: Notation Meaning Example Tilde Measured by a sensor \(\wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\), the gyro output Hat Estimated or computed by the navigator \(\Cmat[\hat]{b}{n}\), the computed attitude \(\delta\) Error, always estimate minus truth: \(\delta x = \hat{x} - x\) \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n}\) \((-)\), \((+)\) Value before / after an update step \(\Cmat{b}{n}(+)\) Subscript \(k\) Sample (epoch) index \(\mathbf{x}_k\) \(\tau_i\) IMU output and integration interval 0.1 s by default

docs.title: Attitude
docs.text:
The vehicle's attitude is the transformation \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) from body axes to NED axes. It can also be described by three Euler angles: roll \(\phi_{nb}\), pitch \(\theta_{nb}\) and heading (yaw) \(\psi_{nb}\). \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) is built by rotating through heading about the Down axis, then pitch about the new y axis, then roll about the new x axis: a z-y-x sequence.

Quaternion component order

Groves writes the attitude quaternion \(\qvec{b}{n}\) scalar-first, \((q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3)\), with \(q_0\) the scalar part. The code stores it scalar-last, [x, y, z, w], because that is the convention of scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation. The two describe the same rotation; only the storage order differs.

docs.title: Position, Earth shape and gravity
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(L_b\) Geodetic latitude of the body \(\lambda_b\) Longitude of the body \(h_b\) Geodetic height above the WGS-84 ellipsoid \(R_0\), \(e\), \(f\) Equatorial radius, eccentricity and flattening of the ellipsoid \(\omega_{ie}\) Earth rotation rate (a scalar). Its vector form in NED is \(\wvec{ie}{n}\). \(R_N\) Meridian radius of curvature: governs north-south motion \(R_E\) Transverse radius of curvature: governs east-west motion \(\gvec{b}{n}\) Acceleration due to gravity at the body, resolved in NED (Down-positive) \[ R_N = \frac{R_0\,(1-e^2)}{\left(1-e^2\sin^2 L_b\right)^{3/2}}, \qquad R_E = \frac{R_0}{\sqrt{1-e^2\sin^2 L_b}} \]

Same letters, different meaning

Many geodesy and navigation texts write the meridian radius as \(M\) or \(R_M\), and the prime-vertical (normal) radius as \(N\) or \(R_N\). In those texts, \(R_N\) is Groves' \(R_E\). ins_sim v0.2 and earlier followed that convention. From v0.3.0 the code and these docs use Groves' \(R_N\) (meridian) and \(R_E\) (transverse).

Height

\(h_b\) is height above the ellipsoid. The simulator has no geoid model, so mission altitudes given above mean sea level (for example the YAML alt_ft key) are used directly as ellipsoidal height.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors are always the estimate minus the truth.

  • Attitude error \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\) is the small rotation that takes the true attitude to the computed one: \(\Cmat[\hat]{b}{n} \approx \left(\Ithree + \skew{\delta\psivec{nb}{n}}\right)\Cmat{b}{n}\). Its components are the North tilt, the East tilt and the Down (heading) error.
  • Velocity error \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n} = \vvec[\hat]{eb}{n} - \vvec{eb}{n}\).
  • Position error \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\), resolved in NED at the true position:
\[ \delta\rvec{eb}{n} = \begin{bmatrix} \left(R_N + h_b\right)\delta L_b \\ \left(R_E + h_b\right)\cos L_b\,\delta\lambda_b \\ -\delta h_b \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: IMU errors
docs.text:
The sensors' outputs are modelled as

\[ \fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_a + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_a\right)\fvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_a, \qquad \wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_g + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_g\right)\wvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_g \]

where each bias is split into a static and a dynamic part, \(\mathbf{b}_a = \mathbf{b}_{as} + \mathbf{b}_{ad}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_g = \mathbf{b}_{gs} + \mathbf{b}_{gd}\).

Term Meaning Drawn IMUSpec field YAML key \(\mathbf{b}_{gs}\), \(\mathbf{b}_{as}\) Static (turn-on) bias Once per trial gyro_br_std, accel_br_std repeatability_* \(\mathbf{b}_{gd}\), \(\mathbf{b}_{ad}\) Dynamic (in-run) bias: a first-order Gauss–Markov process whose Allan deviation peaks at the datasheet bias instability Every sample *_bias_instability, *_bias_tau bias_instab_*, bias_tau_s \(\mathbf{M}_g\), \(\mathbf{M}_a\) Scale factor (diagonal) and misalignment (off-diagonal) Once per trial *_sf_std, *_ma_std scale_factor_ppm, misalignment_urad \(\mathbf{w}_g\), \(\mathbf{w}_a\) White noise: ARW and VRW Every sample gyro_arw, accel_vrw arw_deg_per_rt_hr, vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}(0)\) Initial alignment error Once per trial align_tilt_std, align_heading_std alignment: block

Groves' gyro model also includes a g-dependent bias, proportional to specific force. ins_sim does not model it.

docs.title: Barometer errors
docs.text:
The barometric altimeter that aids the vertical channel reports

\[ \tilde h_b = h_b + s_b\left(h_b - h_{b0}\right) + b_{bs} + b_{bd} + w_b \]

where \(h_{b0}\) is the height of the departure point.

Term Meaning Drawn BaroSpec field YAML key \(s_b\) Scale-factor error, from a non-standard air temperature Once per trial scale_factor_std scale_factor_pct \(b_{bs}\) Static bias, from the altimeter setting (QNH) Once per trial bias_std bias_m \(b_{bd}\) Weather drift: a first-order Gauss–Markov process Every sample drift_std, drift_tau drift_m, drift_tau_s \(w_b\) White noise Every sample noise_density noise_m_per_rt_hz
