\(\mathbf{F}\), \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) Error-state system matrix and state transition matrix – F, Phi – Covariance analysis \(\mathbf{P}\), \(\mathbf{Q}\) Error covariance and process-noise density state units² (per s) P, Q – Covariance analysis

User-facing names do not change: YAML keys, command-line flags and GUI labels keep their datasheet-style names. For example, the GUI's Time step (dt) is \(\tau_i\).

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Everything inside the simulator is SI: radians, metres, seconds, and quantities derived from them. Mission and IMU YAML files use the units of aviation charts and sensor datasheets (degrees, feet, knots, °/h, µg), and are converted to SI as they are loaded. The GUI converts back to familiar display units (degrees, nautical miles) only when plotting.

docs.title: Truth trajectory & ideal IMU
docs.text:
To test a navigator you need to know the right answer. ins_sim builds a truth trajectory from a mission written in YAML: the vehicle's actual position, velocity and attitude at every sample. It then works out what a perfect IMU would have measured along that trajectory. Those ideal gyro and accelerometer outputs feed the IMU error model; the truth itself is what every navigation error is measured against. The mission you pick in the GUI is the one this page builds.

Key results

  • The mission is assembled phase by phase in metres along North, East and Down from the start point. Its velocity is then smoothed, so every manoeuvre starts and ends over a few seconds.
  • The attitude follows the velocity: the nose points along the flight path, and every turn is coordinated. There is no angle of attack, no sideslip and no wind.
  • By default the ideal IMU outputs are computed as the exact inverse of the navigator's basic update. Fed back through the navigator, they reproduce the truth to about \(10^{-8}\) m over the whole mission.
  • The simulator then measures how sensor errors propagate, not how accurately the navigator integrates continuous motion.
  • An oversampled truth instead reports what a real, integrating IMU would: the average rates over each interval of a motion that is continuous within it. Against it the navigator's own integration error shows up.

docs.title: Physical picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Y["Mission YAML<br/>phases"] --> V["Velocity profile<br/>v<sub>eb</sub><sup>n</sup>, smoothed"]
    V --> A["Attitude<br/>from velocity"]
    V --> P["Curvilinear position<br/>L<sub>b</sub>, λ<sub>b</sub>, h<sub>b</sub>"]
    A --> I["Ideal IMU outputs<br/>ω<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>, f<sub>ib</sub><sup>b</sup>"]
    P --> I
    V --> I

A mission is a list of phases flown one after another: a ground roll, the takeoff, a climb, legs to waypoints with optional loiters, and speed changes. Each phase produces a stretch of position and velocity in metres from the start point, in that point's North, East and Down axes:

Phase Motion ground_roll Constant acceleration along the runway heading, up to the rotation speed takeoff Pitch and speed ramp up together over a set time climb Constant speed and flight-path angle, up to a target altitude waypoint A coordinated turn to the waypoint's bearing at the departure's nav_bank_angle_deg, then a straight or climbing leg to it; optionally a loiter of whole circles at a set bank angle speed_ramp A linear change of speed, optionally to a Mach number at the standard-atmosphere temperature of the current altitude

A turn at speed \(v\) and bank angle \(\phi\) has radius \(v^2/(g_0\tan\phi)\), with \(g_0\) = 9.80665 m/s². The phases join with corners in their velocity, so the whole velocity profile is smoothed with a Gaussian filter of 2 s standard deviation. A roll into a turn then takes 4 to 6 s, as it would in a transport aircraft.

docs.title: Attitude from velocity
docs.text:
The truth vehicle flies like an idealized aircraft: its nose points along its velocity, and it banks exactly as much as a coordinated turn needs.

\[ \psi_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}\left(v_E,\, v_N\right), \qquad \theta_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}\left(-v_D,\, v_h\right), \qquad \phi_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}\left(v_h\,\dot\psi_{nb},\, g_\text{ref}\right) \]

where:

  • \(\psi_{nb}\), \(\theta_{nb}\) and \(\phi_{nb}\) are the heading, pitch and roll [rad];
  • \(v_N\), \(v_E\), \(v_D\) are the components of \(\vvec{eb}{n}\), and \(v_h = \sqrt{v_N^2 + v_E^2}\) is the horizontal speed [m/s];
  • \(\dot\psi_{nb}\) is the rate of change of heading [rad/s];
  • \(g_\text{ref}\) is gravity at the departure point [m/s²].

The roll formula is the coordinated-turn condition: the lift, tilted by the bank angle, supplies the centripetal acceleration \(v_h\dot\psi_{nb}\) sideways while still balancing gravity. Nothing pushes the aircraft sideways relative to its own axes, so the lateral accelerometer reads almost zero, even in a turn.

docs.title: What a perfect IMU measures
docs.text:
A perfect gyro triad measures the body's angular rate relative to inertial space, \(\wvec{ib}{b}\). That is the body's rate relative to the NED frame, plus the NED frame's own rotation (Earth rate and transport rate):

\[ \wvec{ib}{b} = \wvec{nb}{b} + \Cmat{n}{b}\left(\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right) \]

A perfect accelerometer triad measures specific force, \(\fvec{ib}{b}\): the acceleration the vehicle needs, relative to the rotating Earth, plus the Coriolis and transport terms, minus gravity:

\[ \fvec{ib}{n} = \vvec[\dot]{eb}{n} + \left(2\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right)\times\vvec{eb}{n} - \gvec{b}{n}, \qquad \fvec{ib}{b} = \Cmat{n}{b}\,\fvec{ib}{n} \]

where \(\Cmat{n}{b} = (\Cmat{b}{n})^{\mathsf T}\) resolves NED vectors in body axes, and \(\gvec{b}{n}\) is gravity (see Earth & gravity). These are the navigation equations solved for the sensor outputs: given the motion, they return the measurements that would produce it.

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
The truth is built on the same time grid as the navigator, one sample per IMU interval \(\tau_i\), and its outputs are written as the exact inverse of the navigator's discrete update rather than of the continuous equations.

1. Smoothing. The phases' velocity profile is low-pass filtered:

EquationCode \[ \vvec{eb}{n}(t) \leftarrow \left(G_\sigma * \vvec{eb}{n}\right)(t), \qquad \sigma = 2~\text{s} \]

where \(G_\sigma\) is a Gaussian kernel and \(*\) is convolution.

_att_sigma = max(1, int(2.0 / tau_i))
all_vel = gaussian_filter1d(all_vel, sigma=_att_sigma, axis=0)

2. Attitude from velocity. The heading rate is a finite difference of the sampled heading:

EquationCode \[ \psi_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}(v_E, v_N), \quad \theta_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}(-v_D, v_h), \quad \phi_{nb} = \operatorname{atan2}(v_h\,\dot\psi_{nb},\, g_\text{ref}) \] 
psi   = np.unwrap(np.arctan2(v_eb_n[:, 1], v_eb_n[:, 0]))
v_h   = np.linalg.norm(v_eb_n[:, :2], axis=1)
theta = np.arctan2(-v_eb_n[:, 2], np.maximum(v_h, 1e-6))
psi_dot = np.gradient(psi, tau_i, edge_order=edge_order)
phi   = np.arctan2(v_h * psi_dot, g_ref)

3. Curvilinear position. Latitude, longitude and height are integrated from the velocity, one forward-Euler step per sample, exactly as the navigator integrates them:

EquationCode \[ L_{b,k+1} = L_{b,k} + \frac{v_{N,k}\,\tau_i}{R_N + h_{b,k}}, \quad \lambda_{b,k+1} = \lambda_{b,k} + \frac{v_{E,k}\,\tau_i}{(R_E + h_{b,k})\cos L_{b,k}}, \quad h_{b,k+1} = h_{b,k} - v_{D,k}\,\tau_i \]

with the radii evaluated at \(L_{b,k}\).

L_b = np.zeros(M); lambda_b = np.zeros(M); h_b = np.zeros(M)
L_b[0], lambda_b[0], h_b[0] = L_b0, lambda_b0, h_b0
for k in range(M - 1):
    R_N, R_E = wgs84_radii(L_b[k])
    L_b[k+1] = L_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k, 0] / (R_N + h_b[k])) * tau_i
    lambda_b[k+1] = lambda_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k, 1] /
                                   ((R_E + h_b[k]) * np.cos(L_b[k]))) * tau_i
    h_b[k+1] = h_b[k] - v_eb_n[k, 2] * tau_i

4. Specific force. The velocity's rate of change over each step is a forward difference, the same difference the navigator's velocity update will take:

EquationCode \[ \fvec{ib}{n}(k) = \frac{\vvec{eb}{n}(k+1) - \vvec{eb}{n}(k)}{\tau_i} + \left(2\wvec{ie}{n} + \wvec{en}{n}\right)_k \times \vvec{eb}{n}(k) - \gvec{b}{n}(k), \qquad \fvec{ib}{b}(k) = \Cmat{n}{b}(k)\,\fvec{ib}{n}(k) \] 
v_eb_n_rate = np.empty((M, 3))
v_eb_n_rate[:-1] = (v_eb_n[1:] - v_eb_n[:-1]) / tau_i
v_eb_n_rate[-1]  = v_eb_n_rate[-2]
f_ib_n = v_eb_n_rate + np.cross(2.0 * omega_ie_n + omega_en_n, v_eb_n) - g_b_n
self.f_ib_b = C_n_b.apply(f_ib_n)

5. Angular rate. The body's rotation over each step is taken from the two attitudes at either end of it, exactly, as a rotation vector:

EquationCode \[ \wvec{nb}{b}(k) = \frac{1}{\tau_i}\operatorname{rotvec}\left(\Cmat{n}{b}(k)\,\Cmat{b}{n}(k+1)\right), \qquad \wvec{ib}{b}(k) = \wvec{nb}{b}(k) + \Cmat{n}{b}(k)\,\wvec{in}{n}(k) \] 
dC_b = self.C_b_n[:-1].inv() * self.C_b_n[1:]       # C_b(k+1)^b(k)
omega_nb_b_fwd = dC_b.as_rotvec() / tau_i            # (M-1, 3)
omega_nb_b = np.vstack([omega_nb_b_fwd, omega_nb_b_fwd[-1:]])
self.omega_ib_b = omega_nb_b + C_n_b.apply(omega_ie_n + omega_en_n)

The navigator undoes each of these steps exactly: its attitude update applies the same rotation vector, its velocity update the same difference, and its position update the same Euler step. The last sample, which has no next sample to difference against, repeats the previous outputs.

Compared with Groves (2013)

The specific force and angular rate are the kinematic definitions of Groves' navigation equations1, solved for the sensor outputs. What is specific to ins_sim is that they are discretized to invert the navigator's own first-order update, so the truth and the navigator agree exactly when the sensors are perfect.

docs.title: Integrating IMU
docs.text:
The default outputs describe a vehicle that moves in jumps, one step at a time. To test how well the navigator integrates continuous motion, ins_sim can instead give the outputs of a real IMU, which integrates the rates over each interval. With oversample set to \(M\), the mission is built at the finer step \(\tau_f = \tau_i/M\), and the truth is the continuous motion through those fine samples: between two of them the body turns relative to NED at a constant rate, the velocity changes at a constant rate, and the specific force in NED is constant, with gravity and the Coriolis term at the mean of their values at the two samples. The states are kept every \(M\)-th sample, and the outputs are the averages of \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) and \(\fvec{ib}{b}\) over each interval \(\tau_i\), which is what an integrating IMU reports.

1. Position, by the trapezoidal rule, since the velocity changes linearly between fine samples:

EquationCode \[ h_{b,j+1} = h_{b,j} - \tfrac12\left(v_{D,j} + v_{D,j+1}\right)\tau_f, \qquad L_{b,j+1} = L_{b,j} + \tfrac12\left(\frac{v_{N,j}}{R_{N,j} + h_{b,j}} + \frac{v_{N,j+1}}{R_{N,j+1} + h_{b,j+1}}\right)\tau_f \]

and likewise for \(\lambda_b\). The radii at the end of the step are taken at a latitude predicted with the start values, which keeps the update second order.

for j in range(n_fine - 1):
    h.append(h[j] - 0.5 * (v_D[j] + v_D[j+1]) * tau_f)
    # Radii at a predicted endpoint latitude keep the update second order.
    L_pred = L[j] + v_N[j] / (R_N + h[j]) * tau_f
    R_N_next, R_E_next = _radii(L_pred)
    L.append(L[j] + 0.5 * (v_N[j] / (R_N + h[j])
                           + v_N[j+1] / (R_N_next + h[j+1])) * tau_f)
    lam.append(lam[j] + 0.5 * (v_E[j] / ((R_E + h[j]) * cos(L[j]))
                               + v_E[j+1] / ((R_E_next + h[j+1]) * cos(L[j+1]))) * tau_f)
    R_N, R_E = _radii(L[j+1])

2. Integrated outputs. Over the fine step \(j\) the body turns through \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_j = \operatorname{rotvec}(\Cmat{n}{b}(j)\,\Cmat{b}{n}(j+1))\) relative to NED, so the NED-to-body matrix is \(\exp(-s\skew{\boldsymbol{\phi}_j})\Cmat{n}{b}(j)\) a fraction \(s\) of the way through it. Averaging that over the step gives the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(-\boldsymbol{\phi}_j)\Cmat{n}{b}(j)\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathbf{x}) = \Ithree + \frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2}\skew{\mathbf{x}} + \frac{x - \sin x}{x^3}\skew{\mathbf{x}}^2\) and \(x = |\mathbf{x}|\):

EquationCode \[ \avec{ib,j}{b} = \boldsymbol{\phi}_j + \tau_f\,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(-\boldsymbol{\phi}_j)\,\Cmat{n}{b}(j)\,\bar{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{in}^n(j), \qquad \uvec{ib,j}{b} = \tau_f\,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(-\boldsymbol{\phi}_j)\,\Cmat{n}{b}(j)\,\fvec{ib}{n}(j) \]

with \(\fvec{ib}{n}(j)\) as in step 4 above, at the fine step, but with gravity and the Coriolis term averaged over the two samples, and \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{in}^n(j)\) the mean of \(\wvec{in}{n}\) at the two samples. The outputs are the sums over the \(M\) fine steps of each interval, divided by \(\tau_i\).

phi = (C_b_n[:-1].inv() * C_b_n[1:]).as_rotvec()     # (n_fine-1, 3)
coriolis_minus_g = np.cross(omega_ie_n + omega_in_n, v_eb_n) - g_b_n
f_ib_n = ((v_eb_n[1:] - v_eb_n[:-1]) / tau_f
          + 0.5 * (coriolis_minus_g[:-1] + coriolis_minus_g[1:]))
omega_in_mid = 0.5 * (omega_in_n[:-1] + omega_in_n[1:])
alpha_fine = phi + tau_f * _gamma_apply(-phi, C_n_b.apply(omega_in_mid))
upsilon_fine = tau_f * _gamma_apply(-phi, C_n_b.apply(f_ib_n))
alpha = alpha_fine.reshape(n_out - 1, oversample, 3).sum(axis=1)
upsilon = upsilon_fine.reshape(n_out - 1, oversample, 3).sum(axis=1)

The truth is still built from fine samples, so it is continuous motion only to the extent that the fine step resolves it. Against it, a navigator at \(\tau_i\) shows its own error plus a floor from the fine step that falls as \(\tau_f\) shrinks: on the packaged mission, about 2 m of horizontal error at \(\tau_f\) = 0.01 s, and 0.6 m at 0.005 s. Keep \(M\) large enough that the floor stays below the error you want to see. The Strapdown mechanization page describes the navigator that integrates these outputs accurately.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
What a perfect IMU measures along the packaged mission, at the app's default \(\tau_i\) = 0.1 s. Every feature has a simple physical reading:

  • Accelerometer z: −9.8 m/s² in level flight, the reaction to gravity. It reaches −11.3 m/s² in the 30° banks of the two loiters, \(g/\cos 30°\), and −10.8 m/s² in the 25° turns to the waypoints. In the 10° climb it is \(-g\cos 10°\) = −9.6 m/s².
  • Accelerometer x: the takeoff run, then +1.7 m/s² during the climb, where the pitched-up accelerometer feels \(g\sin 10°\) of gravity. Later come the two speed changes.
  • Accelerometer y stays close to zero throughout, because every turn is coordinated.
  • Gyros: in a banked turn the turn rate splits between the body's z axis (\(\dot\psi_{nb}\cos\phi_{nb}\)) and its y axis (\(\dot\psi_{nb}\sin\phi_{nb}\)). The x gyro shows the brief roll into and out of each turn.

Earth rate, 15 °/h or 0.004 °/s, is in the gyro outputs too, but far too small to see at this scale.

The zero-noise round trip on the Validation page feeds these outputs back through the navigator, which reproduces the truth to \(2.3 \times 10^{-8}\) m. The Strapdown mechanization page plots that residual.

docs.title: Assumptions & limitations
docs.text:
Assumptions & limitations

  • Point-mass flight. The body axes follow the velocity: no angle of attack, no sideslip, no wind, no vibration, and no lever arm between the IMU and the vehicle's reference point.
  • No integration error to find, by default. The default outputs are piecewise constant over each step and invert the navigator's own basic discretization. The navigator's integration errors, such as coning, sculling and its first-order velocity update, are therefore invisible: the simulator behaves as if the navigation algorithm were perfect. An oversampled truth makes them visible.
  • The sample interval shows up in turns. The specific force is the forward difference across a step, so during a turn it has a small component along the direction of flight, about \(-v_h\dot\psi_{nb}^2\tau_i/2\). At \(\tau_i\) = 1 s that is about −0.1 m/s² in the loiters, as the example below prints; at 0.1 s it is ten times smaller. The navigator undoes it exactly.
  • Waypoints are approximate. Bearings and distances to waypoints use a spherical Earth, and legs are straight lines in the start point's NED axes, so a distant waypoint is reached only approximately.
  • Standard atmosphere. Mach numbers are converted to speed with the ISA temperature at the current altitude. The departure altitude, given above mean sea level, is used as the ellipsoidal height.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text:
Quantity Equation Implemented in Mission phases and smoothing Phase table, \(G_\sigma * \vvec{eb}{n}\) build_trajectory Attitude from velocity \(\psi_{nb}\), \(\theta_{nb}\), \(\phi_{nb}\) _euler_from_velocity in ins_sim/trajectory/kinematics.py Curvilinear position Forward-Euler \(L_b\), \(\lambda_b\), \(h_b\) TruthTrajectory Ideal IMU outputs \(\fvec{ib}{b}\), \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) TruthTrajectory Integrating IMU \(\avec{ib}{b}\), \(\uvec{ib}{b}\) over each interval oversample in TruthTrajectory and build_trajectory Smooth test paths Cubic spline through NED waypoints, flown at constant speed NEDSplinePath, TruthTrajectory.from_spline

This example builds the packaged mission at \(\tau_i\) = 1 s, prints the ideal accelerometer output in level flight and in the most steeply banked turn, and runs the zero-noise round trip:

ScriptOutput 
"""What a perfect IMU measures along the packaged mission, and the zero-noise round trip."""

import numpy as np

from ins_sim.config import default_trajectory_path
from ins_sim.navigation.strapdown import NavState, strapdown_navgrade
from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory

np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True, floatmode="fixed")

truth, _, _ = build_trajectory(str(default_trajectory_path()), tau_i=1.0)
roll = truth.euler_nb[:, 0]

# Straight and level at Mach 0.8 (75 minutes in): the accelerometers sense
# the reaction to gravity, along the body z axis, and almost nothing else.
k = int(np.searchsorted(truth.t, 75 * 60.0))
print(f"t = {truth.t[k] / 60:2.0f} min, roll {np.rad2deg(roll[k]):4.1f}°: "
      f"f_ib^b = {truth.f_ib_b[k].round(3) + 0.0} m/s²")

# An hour in, the aircraft is in its most steeply banked turn. The specific
# force tilts with the aircraft, so it stays on the body z axis and grows
# to g / cos(roll).
k = int(np.searchsorted(truth.t, 60 * 60.0))
print(f"t = {truth.t[k] / 60:2.0f} min, roll {np.rad2deg(roll[k]):4.1f}°: "
      f"f_ib^b = {truth.f_ib_b[k].round(3) + 0.0} m/s²")
print(f"g / cos(roll) = {truth.g[k] / np.cos(roll[k]):.3f} m/s²")

# The ideal outputs are the exact inverse of the navigator's update, so
# navigating with them reproduces the truth.
start = NavState(truth.L_b[0], truth.lambda_b[0], truth.h_b[0],
                 truth.v_eb_n[0], truth.C_b_n[0].as_quat())
nav = strapdown_navgrade(truth.omega_ib_b, truth.f_ib_b, start, truth.tau_i,
                         meas_h_b=truth.h_b)
largest = np.abs(nav.r_lb_l - truth.r_lb_l).max()
print(f"Round trip reproduces the truth to within a micrometre: {bool(largest < 1e-6)}")

t = 75 min, roll  0.0°: f_ib^b = [ 0.000 -0.008 -9.782] m/s²
t = 60 min, roll 30.0°: f_ib^b = [ -0.104   0.012 -11.259] m/s²
g / cos(roll) = 11.281 m/s²
Round trip reproduces the truth to within a micrometre: True

In level flight the accelerometers also sense 0.008 m/s² sideways and a little more than gravity vertically. Holding a constant velocity relative to the rotating, curved Earth is an accelerated motion in inertial space, and those are the Coriolis and transport terms of the specific force.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Groves (2013), Chapter 2, for specific force and the kinematics of rotating frames, and Chapter 5 for the navigation equations that the ideal outputs invert. ↩

docs.title: Vertical channel
docs.text:
Height is the one direction in which an INS cannot navigate on its own for long. Gravity weakens with height, so a navigator that believes it is higher than it is computes too little gravity. The resulting acceleration error pushes it higher still, and the error grows exponentially, with a time constant of under ten minutes. Every practical INS therefore blends in a height measurement, usually from a barometric altimeter. ins_sim does this with a third-order damping loop, which is on by default. Untick Baro altitude aiding in the GUI to watch the free-inertial vertical channel diverge.

Key results

  • Free-inertial, a height error grows as \(\sinh(t/\tau_v)\), with \(\tau_v\) = 573 s at the equator. A 1 m/s vertical-velocity error becomes 6.6 km of height error in 30 minutes.
  • The barometric loop places all three of its poles at \(-1/\tau\), with \(\tau\) = 100 s. The same 1 m/s error then causes a 23 m transient that dies away within about 20 minutes.
  • The loop's integrator cancels a constant vertical accelerometer bias.
  • The INS height follows the barometer, errors included. A constant barometer error ends up in full in the INS height, a slow drift is followed with a lag, and white noise is filtered down to \(1.44\,N/\sqrt\tau\). With the packaged spec the barometer, not the IMU, sets the Down position error.

docs.title: Physical picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    BARO["Barometric height<br/>h̃<sub>b</sub>"] --> SUM(("−"))
    INS["INS height<br/>h<sub>b</sub>"] --> SUM
    SUM -->|"residual"| K1["K<sub>1</sub>: correct the height"]
    SUM --> K2["K<sub>2</sub>: correct the vertical velocity"]
    SUM --> K3["K<sub>3</sub>: integrate into a<br/>vertical-acceleration correction"]

Without a height reference, the vertical channel is a positive feedback loop. A height error \(\delta h_b\) makes the computed gravity wrong by the free-air gradient, \(-(2g/R_0)\,\delta h_b\): too weak if the navigator is too high. Too little gravity means a computed upward acceleration, which makes the height error grow faster.

With a barometric altimeter, the navigator compares its height with the barometer's and feeds the difference back into three places: the height itself, the vertical velocity, and an integrator that learns any steady vertical-acceleration error, such as an accelerometer bias.

docs.title: The free-inertial instability
docs.text:
Linearizing the vertical velocity equation about the true trajectory gives the height error's dynamics:

\[ \delta\ddot h_b = \left(\frac{2g}{R_0} - 4\,\omega_{ie}^2\cos^2 L_b\right)\delta h_b - \delta f_D = \frac{\delta h_b}{\tau_v^2} - \delta f_D \]

where:

  • \(\delta h_b\) is the height error [m] and \(\delta f_D\) the error in the Down specific force [m/s²];
  • \(R_0\) is the equatorial radius [m] and \(\omega_{ie}\) the Earth rotation rate [rad/s];
  • \(\tau_v\) is the time constant of the divergence [s].

The first term is the gravity gradient. The second, much smaller, is Coriolis coupling: a vertical velocity error causes an East velocity error through the Earth's rotation, which in turn feeds back into the vertical. From a vertical velocity error \(\delta v_D(0)\) and no other error,

\[ \delta h_b(t) = -\delta v_D(0)\,\tau_v\sinh\frac{t}{\tau_v}, \qquad \tau_v = \left(\frac{2g}{R_0} - 4\,\omega_{ie}^2\cos^2 L_b\right)^{-1/2} \approx 573~\text{s} \]

and from a constant Down accelerometer bias \(b_D\), \(\delta h_b(t) = -b_D\,\tau_v^2\left(\cosh(t/\tau_v) - 1\right)\). Both grow by a factor of \(e\) every 9.5 minutes.

docs.title: The barometric damping loop
docs.text:
Writing \(\tilde h_b\) for the barometric height, the loop adds three corrections, driven by the residual \(r = h_b - \tilde h_b\):

\[ \dot h_b = -v_D - K_1\,r, \qquad \dot v_D = \left(\dot v_D\right)_\text{inertial} + K_2\,r + a_c, \qquad \dot a_c = K_3\,r \] \[ K_1 = \frac{3}{\tau}, \qquad K_2 = \frac{3}{\tau^2}, \qquad K_3 = \frac{1}{\tau^3} \]

where:

  • \(r\) is the residual, INS height minus barometric height [m];
  • \(\left(\dot v_D\right)_\text{inertial}\) is the Down component of the velocity equation on Strapdown mechanization [m/s²];
  • \(a_c\) is the integrator's vertical-acceleration correction [m/s²];
  • \(\tau\) is the loop's time constant, 100 s by default [s].

If the INS is too high (\(r > 0\)), the loop lowers its height directly through \(K_1\), commands a descent through \(K_2\), and slowly builds up a downward acceleration through \(K_3\). With an ideal barometer the residual is the height error itself, and the closed loop's error dynamics have the characteristic polynomial

\[ s^3 + K_1 s^2 + \left(K_2 - \frac{2g}{R_0}\right)s + K_3 \approx \left(s + \frac{1}{\tau}\right)^3 \]

The gravity gradient \(2g/R_0\) is only 1% of \(K_2\) at \(\tau\) = 100 s, so the three poles sit very close to \(-1/\tau\): critically damped, without oscillation. For a vertical velocity error \(\delta v_D(0)\) the height error is then

\[ \delta h_b(t) \approx -\delta v_D(0)\,t\,e^{-t/\tau}\left(1 - \frac{t}{2\tau}\right) \]

which reaches \(-0.23\,\delta v_D(0)\,\tau\) at \(t = 0.59\,\tau\), changes sign at \(t = 2\tau\), and overshoots by \(+0.08\,\delta v_D(0)\,\tau\) at \(t = 3.4\,\tau\). A constant accelerometer bias leaves no steady height error: the integrator settles at \(a_c = -b_D\).

docs.title: Barometer errors
docs.text:
A pressure altimeter measures static pressure and converts it to height through a standard atmosphere, so its height is wrong whenever the day's atmosphere differs from that standard1. ins_sim models the barometric height as

\[ \tilde h_b = h_b + s_b\left(h_b - h_{b0}\right) + b_{bs} + b_{bd}(t) + w_b \]

where:

  • \(h_{b0}\) is the height of the departure point [m]. There the altimeter setting makes the barometer read correctly, apart from \(b_{bs}\);
  • \(s_b\) is the scale-factor error [dimensionless]. Air colder than standard is denser, so pressure falls off faster with height, and the altimeter misreads the height above the departure point by about \(\Delta T/T\);
  • \(b_{bs}\) is the static bias [m], from the error in the altimeter setting (QNH) and the sensor's offset;
  • \(b_{bd}\) is the weather drift [m], a first-order Gauss–Markov process, the same model as the in-run biases on the IMU error model page;
  • \(w_b\) is white noise of density \(N\) [m/√Hz].

Writing \(e = \tilde h_b - h_b\) for the barometer's error, the residual is \(r = \delta h_b - e\). The loop equations above then give the INS height error as \(e\) passed through a filter:

\[ \frac{\delta h_b(s)}{e(s)} = \frac{K_1 s^2 + K_2 s + K_3}{s^3 + K_1 s^2 + \left(K_2 - 1/\tau_v^2\right)s + K_3} \approx \frac{3\tau^2 s^2 + 3\tau s + 1}{\left(\tau s + 1\right)^3} \]

Its gain at \(s = 0\) is exactly 1, gravity gradient included. That has three consequences:

  • A constant error ends up in full in the INS height. After a step \(e_0\), the height error is \(e_0\left[1 - e^{-t/\tau}\left(1 - 2t/\tau + t^2/2\tau^2\right)\right]\). It overshoots by 21% at \(t = 1.27\,\tau\), then settles on \(e_0\): the navigator cannot tell a barometer bias from a true height.
  • A slow drift is followed with a lag. Drifts much slower than \(\tau\) pass almost unchanged; the faster the drift, the further the INS height lags behind it.
  • White noise is filtered. The INS height error becomes stationary noise with the spread below, where \(h(t)\) is the filter's impulse response.
\[ \sigma_{\delta h} = N\sqrt{\int_0^\infty h(t)^2\,dt} \approx \sqrt{\frac{33}{16}}\,\frac{N}{\sqrt\tau} \approx 1.44\,\frac{N}{\sqrt\tau} \]

With \(N\) = 0.1 m/√Hz and \(\tau\) = 100 s that is 1.4 cm, against 0.32 m per sample from the barometer itself at 10 Hz.

The scale factor and the bias are fixed for a run, and the weather drift is much slower than the loop, so all three pass almost in full into the INS height. With the packaged spec, on a mission that climbs 4.5 km, the scale factor alone gives about 90 m (1σ).

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
1. Barometric height. run_monte_carlo draws each trial's barometer errors from a random stream of their own, so switching them on leaves the IMU and alignment errors of every trial unchanged:

EquationCode \[ \tilde h_b = h_b + s_b\left(h_b - h_{b0}\right) + b_{bs} + b_{bd} + w_b, \qquad \sigma_{w_b} = N/\sqrt{\tau_i} \] 
s_b = rng.normal(0.0, spec.scale_factor_std)
b_bs = rng.normal(0.0, spec.bias_std)
b_bd = gauss_markov(rng, len(h_b), tau_i, spec.drift_std, spec.drift_tau,
                    n_axes=1)[:, 0]
w_b = rng.normal(0.0, spec.noise_density / np.sqrt(tau_i), size=len(h_b))
return h_b + s_b * (h_b - h_b[0]) + b_bs + b_bd + w_b

2. Gains, set once from baro_tau:

EquationCode \[ K_1 = \frac{3}{\tau}, \qquad K_2 = \frac{3}{\tau^2}, \qquad K_3 = \frac{1}{\tau^3} \] 
# Third-order baro-damping gains: triple pole at -1/baro_tau for the
# (height error, vertical-velocity error, accel-error integrator) loop.
if meas_h_b is not None:
    K1 = 3.0 / baro_tau
    K2 = 3.0 / baro_tau ** 2
    K3 = 1.0 / baro_tau ** 3
    acc_corr = 0.0                 # integral state [m/s²], → -δa_D

3. Vertical velocity and integrator. Inside the velocity update, the residual corrects the Down acceleration through \(K_2\) and the integrator, and the integrator accumulates \(K_3\,r\):

EquationCode \[ v_{D,k+1} = v_{D,k} + \left[\left(\dot v_D\right)_\text{inertial} + K_2\,r_k + a_{c,k}\right]\tau_i, \qquad a_{c,k+1} = a_{c,k} + K_3\,r_k\,\tau_i \] 
# --- 5. Rotating-frame velocity update ------------------------
coriolis = np.cross(2.0 * omega_ie_n + omega_en_n, v_eb_n[k])
v_eb_n_dot = f_ib_n - coriolis + g_b_n
# Baro damping: the height residual corrects vertical velocity
# (K2) and updates the accel-error integrator (K3); a positive
# residual (INS high) commands positive Down velocity.
if meas_h_b is not None:
    baro_residual = h_b[k] - meas_h_b[k]
    v_eb_n_dot[2] += K2 * baro_residual + acc_corr
    acc_corr += K3 * baro_residual * tau_i
v_eb_n[k+1] = v_eb_n[k] + v_eb_n_dot * tau_i

4. Height. Inside the position update, the residual corrects the height through \(K_1\):

EquationCode \[ h_{b,k+1} = h_{b,k} - v_{D,k}\,\tau_i - K_1\,r_k\,\tau_i \] 
# --- 6. Curvilinear position (forward Euler — matches truth) --
R_N, R_E = wgs84_radii(L_b[k])
L_b[k+1] = L_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k][0] / (R_N + h_b[k])) * tau_i
lambda_b[k+1] = lambda_b[k] + (v_eb_n[k][1] /
                               ((R_E + h_b[k]) * np.cos(L_b[k]))) * tau_i
h_b[k+1] = h_b[k] - v_eb_n[k][2] * tau_i
if meas_h_b is not None:
    h_b[k+1] -= K1 * baro_residual * tau_i

Compared with Groves (2013)

Groves1 explains the vertical channel's instability and barometric height measurement, and combines sensors with Kalman filters. ins_sim instead uses a classical fixed-gain, third-order baro-inertial loop2, with its gains chosen to place a triple pole.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
A level IMU at rest at the equator, with a 1 m/s Down-velocity error and no other error. Free-inertial, the height error follows the \(\sinh\) prediction, reaching 6.6 km after 30 minutes; its fitted time constant is within 0.1% of \(\tau_v\). With the barometric loop it peaks at 23 m and decays, as the closed form above predicts. Both are checks on the Validation page.

The same IMU at rest, now with a barometer that errs. On the left, a constant 10 m barometer error: the INS height overshoots by about 21% and settles on 10 m. On the right, a fast barometer drift, 10 m correlated over 10 minutes: the INS height follows it a little late, as the filter above predicts. Both are checks on the Validation page.

docs.title: Assumptions & limitations
docs.text:
Assumptions & limitations

  • A simple barometer model. The temperature error is one scale factor for the whole flight, and the weather one Gauss–Markov drift. Real errors follow the route's actual weather, and an aircraft's static-pressure ports add errors that change with speed and attitude. Without a baro block in the IMU spec the barometer is ideal, and the aided vertical errors are then optimistic.
  • Fixed gains. The loop does not adapt to the quality of the barometer; \(\tau\) is fixed at 100 s in the GUI. The Python API accepts other values through baro_tau.
  • Coupling neglected in the closed forms. The pole placement ignores the gravity gradient and the Coriolis coupling with the East channel. The simulation includes both, which is why it departs from the closed form by about 1%.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text:
Quantity Equation Implemented in Loop gains and corrections \(K_1\), \(K_2\), \(K_3\), \(a_c\) strapdown_navgrade, arguments meas_h_b and baro_tau Barometric height \(\tilde h_b\) generate_baro_samples; run_monte_carlo, argument baro_aiding Barometer error spreads \(s_b\), \(b_{bs}\), \(b_{bd}\), \(N\) BaroSpec, the baro block of the IMU spec Weather drift \(b_{bd}\) gauss_markov Gravity gradient \(-2g/R_0\) normal_gravity

This example applies a 1 m/s Down-velocity error to a level IMU at rest at the equator and compares the simulated height error with both closed forms:

ScriptOutput 
"""A 1 m/s Down-velocity error, free-inertial and with an ideal barometer."""

import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

from ins_sim.core.earth_model import WGS84_A, WGS84_OMEGA, earth_rate_n, normal_gravity
from ins_sim.navigation.strapdown import NavState, strapdown_navgrade

L_b, tau_i, M = 0.0, 1.0, 1801                       # 30 minutes at the equator
g = normal_gravity(L_b, 0.0)
omega_ib_b = np.tile(earth_rate_n(L_b), (M, 1))      # a level IMU at rest
f_ib_b = np.tile([0.0, 0.0, -g], (M, 1))
start = NavState(L_b, 0.0, 0.0, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]),   # v_D wrong by 1 m/s
                 Rotation.identity().as_quat())

free = strapdown_navgrade(omega_ib_b, f_ib_b, start, tau_i).h_b
aided = strapdown_navgrade(omega_ib_b, f_ib_b, start, tau_i, meas_h_b=np.zeros(M)).h_b

tau_v = 1.0 / np.sqrt(2.0 * g / WGS84_A - 4.0 * WGS84_OMEGA**2)   # free-inertial
tau = 100.0                                                       # baro loop
print(f"Free-inertial time constant tau_v = {tau_v:.1f} s")
print("Height error [m]  free-inertial           baro-aided")
print("t [min]           simulated  predicted    simulated  predicted")
for minutes in (2, 5, 10, 20, 30):
    t = minutes * 60.0
    k = int(t / tau_i)
    predicted_free = -tau_v * np.sinh(t / tau_v)
    predicted_aided = -t * np.exp(-t / tau) * (1.0 - t / (2.0 * tau))
    print(f"{minutes:7d}         {free[k]:10.1f} {predicted_free:10.1f}"
          f"   {round(aided[k], 1) + 0.0:10.1f} {round(predicted_aided, 1) + 0.0:10.1f}")

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A simulator is only useful if it is right. This page checks ins_sim against results that can be worked out on paper: the textbook behaviour of inertial navigation errors, and the defining statistics of the sensor noise models.

Each check runs the simulator's own code (the same truth generator, IMU error model and strapdown navigator the app uses) on a scenario simple enough to have an exact answer, usually a stationary IMU with exactly one error source. The test suite asserts every agreement on each commit, and the figures and table below are regenerated from the same scenarios. The predictions are derived on the Theory pages: the INS error model, the Vertical channel, the Strapdown mechanization, the IMU error model and the Covariance analysis.

Key results

  • Every inertial check agrees with its prediction to within 0.3%, and every noise check to within statistical sampling error.
  • Barometer errors reach the INS height exactly as the damping loop's transfer function predicts: a bias in full, a drift with a lag, and white noise attenuated about sevenfold at a 1 s step.
  • On an integrating IMU's outputs, the coning and sculling drifts of the basic mechanization match their closed-form predictions, and the precision mechanization cuts each by more than 300 times, again as predicted. Its error falls with at least the square of the step.
  • A 0.01 °/h gyro bias starts the position drifting at about 0.6 nmi/h, the classic figure for a navigation-grade INS. Over hours the Earth-rate loop bends that drift over, and the simulator reproduces the bend too.
  • The bias instability in an IMU spec is the datasheet value. ins_sim models the in-run bias with a Gauss–Markov process whose spread it sets to \(B/0.617\), so the simulated bias's Allan deviation peaks at exactly \(B\) (see Allan deviation).
  • The covariance analysis follows a single navigator trial to within 1%, and the spreads of 200 Monte Carlo trials of the packaged mission lie within the 95% sampling band of its prediction, 34 times out of 36.

docs.title: How the checks are set up
docs.text:
The inertial checks use a level IMU at rest at the equator, facing North. There the vertical component of Earth rate is zero, so the Foucault effect (Earth rate slowly swapping error between the North and East channels) vanishes, and the single-axis textbook formulas apply exactly. The truth's own perfect IMU outputs, plus the one error under test, go through the navigator:

Code 
est_C_b_n0 = Rot.from_rotvec(delta_psi_nb_n0) * truth.C_b_n[0]
start = NavState(truth.L_b[0], truth.lambda_b[0], truth.h_b[0],
                 truth.v_eb_n[0] + np.asarray(delta_v_eb_n0, dtype=float),
                 est_C_b_n0.as_quat())
nav = strapdown_navgrade(truth.omega_ib_b + np.asarray(gyro_bias_b, dtype=float),
                         truth.f_ib_b + np.asarray(accel_bias_b, dtype=float),
                         start, truth.tau_i,
                         meas_h_b=(truth.h_b if meas_h_b is None else meas_h_b)
                         if baro else None)

Errors are the estimate minus the truth, resolved along North, East and Down at the true position: \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\) for position and \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\) for attitude (see Notation & conventions). The scenarios live in tools/validation_scenarios.py; the assertions in tests/validation/.

docs.title: Zero-noise round trip
docs.text: The truth trajectory's IMU outputs are defined as the exact inverse of the navigator's update, so feeding them back through the navigator must reproduce the truth. On the packaged mission the largest difference is a few times \(10^{-8}\) m, numerical precision. This proves that the truth generator and the navigator are consistent with each other. It does not measure how accurately the navigator integrates continuous motion, because the truth is itself defined by the same discrete steps.

docs.title: Schuler oscillation
docs.text:
A tilted INS misreads part of gravity as horizontal acceleration. The resulting position error moves the computed local vertical, which reduces the tilt: a pendulum with the Earth's radius as its length, the Schuler loop. An initial North tilt \(\delta\psi_N(0)\) sets the East channel oscillating:

\[ \delta r_E(t) = (R_E + h_b)\,\delta\psi_N(0)\,\bigl(1 - \cos\omega_s t\bigr), \qquad \omega_s = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R_E + h_b}}, \qquad T_s = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_s} \]

where:

  • \(\delta r_E\) is the East position error [m];
  • \(R_E\) is the transverse radius of curvature and \(h_b\) the height [m];
  • \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity [m/s²];
  • \(\omega_s\) is the Schuler frequency [rad/s] and \(T_s\) its period [s].

A 20″ tilt produces up to 1.3 km of position error, yet the error never grows past that: it returns to zero every 84.6 minutes.

docs.title: Accelerometer bias
docs.text:
A constant accelerometer bias \(b_a\) is balanced, on average, by a tilt of \(b_a/g\). The position error oscillates about a fixed offset and does not grow:

\[ \delta r_N(t) = \frac{b_a}{\omega_s^2}\,\bigl(1 - \cos\omega_s t\bigr), \qquad \omega_s = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R_N + h_b}} \]

where \(b_a\) is the North accelerometer bias [m/s²] and \(R_N\) the meridian radius of curvature [m].

docs.title: Gyro bias
docs.text:
A constant gyro bias \(b_g\) is different: it keeps rotating the computed attitude, so the position error grows. At first it grows at the rate \((R_N + h_b)\,b_g\), about 0.6 nmi/h for 0.01 °/h. Over hours a second loop bends it over. The North position error is a latitude error, which misresolves Earth rate into a heading error that feeds back into the tilt. Solving the coupled tilt, heading, velocity and latitude error equations at the equator gives:

\[ \delta r_N(t) = -(R_N + h_b)\,b_g\, \frac{\omega_s^2}{\omega_s^2 - \omega_{ie}^2} \left(\frac{\sin\omega_{ie}t}{\omega_{ie}} - \frac{\sin\omega_s t}{\omega_s}\right) \]

where \(b_g\) is the East-axis gyro bias [rad/s] and \(\omega_{ie}\) the Earth rotation rate [rad/s]. While \(\omega_{ie}t\) is small this reduces to the single-channel result \(-(R_N + h_b)\,b_g\,(t - \sin\omega_s t/\omega_s)\).

The Earth-rate loop is real physics

After three hours the single-channel approximation overstates the error by about 10%. The simulation follows the full prediction to within 0.1%: the simulator's rotating-Earth terms produce this coupling without being told about it.

docs.title: Vertical channel
docs.text:
Gravity weakens with height, so an INS that thinks it is too low also thinks gravity is too strong, and accelerates downward: the vertical channel is unstable. With no external height reference, a Down-velocity error \(\delta v_D(0)\) grows as

\[ \delta h(t) = -\delta v_D(0)\,\tau_v\sinh\frac{t}{\tau_v}, \qquad \tau_v = \left(\frac{2g}{R_0} - 4\,\omega_{ie}^2\cos^2 L_b\right)^{-1/2} \]

where \(R_0\) is the equatorial radius [m] and \(L_b\) the latitude [rad]. The \(\omega_{ie}\) term is Coriolis coupling between the Down and East velocity errors, which slows the divergence slightly. With an ideal barometer, the third-order damping loop instead holds the error to a transient of a few tens of metres.

docs.title: Barometer errors
docs.text:
The damping loop pulls the INS height onto the barometer's, errors included. Linearized, the INS height error is the barometer error \(e\) passed through the filter

\[ \frac{\delta h_b(s)}{e(s)} = \frac{K_1 s^2 + K_2 s + K_3}{s^3 + K_1 s^2 + \left(K_2 - 1/\tau_v^2\right)s + K_3} \]

derived on the Vertical channel page. The checks run each kind of barometer error on its own through the navigator and compare the height error with that filter's response:

  • A constant 10 m error must end up in full in the INS height, after the filter's step response.
  • A drift, here one Gauss–Markov realization with a 10 m spread and a 10-minute correlation time, must be followed with the filter's lag. The prediction passes the same realization through the filter.
  • White noise of density \(N\) must leave a height-error spread of \(N\sqrt{\int_0^\infty h(t)^2\,dt}\), where \(h(t)\) is the filter's impulse response. The scenario computes the integral exactly from the filter's state-space form.
Prediction 
K1, K2, K3 = 3.0 / baro_tau, 3.0 / baro_tau**2, 1.0 / baro_tau**3
tau_v = vertical_time_constant(L_b)
num = [K1, K2, K3]
den = [1.0, K1, K2 - 1.0 / tau_v**2, K3]

docs.title: Precision mechanization
docs.text:
These checks feed the navigator the outputs of an integrating IMU, the averages of the angular rate and specific force over each interval, computed exactly for motions with a closed form. The basic mechanization then shows the errors that the precision mechanization exists to remove.

Coning and sculling. In classical coning, the body's z axis traces a cone of half-angle \(\beta\) at frequency \(\Omega\). In classical sculling, the body yaws by \(\theta_0\cos\Omega t\) while accelerating North at \(A\cos\Omega t\). Both rectify: a rotation that oscillates in phase with a second rotation, or with a specific force, drives a steady drift along a third axis. Over each interval, with \(x = \Omega\tau_i\), an update that treats the increments as constant misses

\[ d_0(x) = \tfrac12\left(x - \sin x\right) \]

per unit amplitude, and the one-sample-plus-previous correction leaves

\[ d_1(x) = \tfrac12\left(x - \sin x\right) - \tfrac{1}{12}\left(2\sin x - \sin 2x\right) \approx \frac{x^5}{60}. \]

The heading therefore drifts at \(-\sin^2\beta\,d(x)/\tau_i\) under coning, and the East velocity at \(-(\theta_0 A/\Omega)\,d(x)/\tau_i\) under sculling, with \(d = d_0\) for the basic mechanization and \(d = d_1\) for the precision one. The derivation keeps the lowest order in \(\beta\) and \(\theta_0\), which is exact to well within the checks' tolerance at 1°.

Prediction 
missed = 0.5 * (x - np.sin(x))
if compensated:
    missed -= (2.0 * np.sin(x) - np.sin(2.0 * x)) / 12.0
return float(missed)

The packaged mission. Built with its truth oversampled ten times per step, the packaged mission becomes the output of an integrating IMU. With perfect sensors, the remaining position error is the mechanization's own:

The basic mechanization's error grows in every turn, as the rotation term \(\tfrac12\,\avec{ib}{b}\times\uvec{ib}{b}\) it leaves out predicts. The precision mechanization stays within a few metres, the floor set by the truth's own fine step (see Integrating IMU).

Convergence. Building every truth at the same fine step and changing only the IMU interval shows each mechanization's order: the basic error is proportional to \(\tau_i\), and the precision error falls at least as fast as \(\tau_i^2\) until it meets the floor.

docs.title: Angle random walk
docs.text:
Gyro white noise integrates into an attitude error whose spread grows with the square root of time, at a rate set by the angle random walk (ARW) alone:

\[ \sigma_\theta(t) = \mathrm{ARW}\,\sqrt{t} \]

The per-sample noise is scaled by \(1/\sqrt{\tau_i}\), so the result does not depend on the sample interval \(\tau_i\). Both simulations below follow the same curve.

docs.title: Gauss–Markov bias
docs.text: The in-run bias is a first-order Gauss–Markov process with spread \(\sigma\) and correlation time \(\tau_c\). It starts in its stationary distribution, so its spread across runs is \(\sigma\) from the first sample, and its correlation with itself decays as \(e^{-\Delta t/\tau_c}\).

docs.title: Allan deviation
docs.text:
The Allan deviation is how sensor datasheets characterize noise. For white noise of density \(N\) (the ARW) plus a Gauss–Markov bias it is

\[ \sigma_A^2(T) = \frac{N^2}{T} + \frac{\sigma^2\tau_c^2}{T^2}\left(\frac{2T}{\tau_c} - 3 + 4e^{-T/\tau_c} - e^{-2T/\tau_c}\right) \]

where \(T\) is the averaging time [s]. The Gauss–Markov term peaks at \(0.617\,\sigma\) when \(T = 1.89\,\tau_c\). ins_sim sets \(\sigma = B/0.617\) from the datasheet bias instability \(B\), so the peak lands on \(B\) itself: 0.01 °/h for the packaged spec. The simulated gyro reproduces the whole curve across five decades of \(T\).

Entering bias instability from a datasheet

Enter the bias_instab_* values exactly as the datasheet gives them: the floor of the sensor's Allan deviation. ins_sim converts each to the spread of its Gauss–Markov model, \(\sigma = B/0.617\), so that the simulated Allan deviation peaks at \(B\) at an averaging time of \(1.89\,\tau_c\). Choose bias_tau_s so that the peak falls where the datasheet's Allan floor is: \(\tau_c \approx T_\text{floor}/1.89\).

Some datasheets quote the IEEE 952 bias-instability coefficient rather than the floor itself. The floor is 0.664 times that coefficient, so multiply by 0.664 before entering it.

docs.title: Initial attitude error
docs.text: Each Monte Carlo trial draws its alignment error from its own random stream, and the attitude error at the first sample must equal that draw. tests/evaluation/test_monte_carlo.py checks it to \(10^{-12}\) rad.

docs.title: Covariance analysis
docs.text:
The covariance analysis predicts the spread of the navigation errors from a linearized error model. Two checks test it: one against the navigator, one against the Monte Carlo.

One trial, no randomness. A turning, climbing 20-minute flight at \(\tau_i\) = 0.1 s, with one draw of every constant error of the packaged IMU spec: alignment, turn-on biases, scale factors, misalignments and the barometer's scale factor and bias. The same initial errors, propagated by the covariance analysis's state transition matrices, follow the navigator's nine errors to within the share of their largest values given in the table above. Any wrong sign or missing term in the error model would show here at full size.

Many trials. The packaged mission at \(\tau_i\) = 1 s, with every error source, flown 200 times. The trials' spread of each error is its RMS over the trials, which the linear model predicts to be centred on zero. With \(N\) trials it is uncertain by about \(1/\sqrt{2N}\), so 95% of the ratios to the prediction should lie within \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{2N}\) = ±0.098 of 1.

Of the 36 ratios, 34 lie inside the band, about what a 95% band leads one to expect. They lean a few percent above 1 together, because all nine errors of a trial come from the same few random draws: a few unusually large draws among these 200 trials raise the spread of many errors at once. With other seeds the lean goes the other way; 100 trials with seeds 11 and 23 give mean ratios of 0.999 and 0.989.

The CEP is a median, not an RMS, so its check uses an interval that assumes nothing about how the errors are distributed. The number of trials below the true median is binomial, \(B(N, \tfrac12)\), so the sorted trials themselves bound it: with 200 trials, the 86th and 115th smallest horizontal errors bracket it with 96% confidence. The predicted CEP at the end of the flight lies inside that interval (table above). The covariance analysis takes about 3 s for this mission; the 200 trials took 4 minutes.

docs.title: Rerunning the checks
docs.text:
python -m pytest tests/validation             # assert every agreement
python tools/generate_doc_plots.py --validation  # redraw the figures and the table

The derivations follow Groves (2013) and Titterton & Weston (2004); the Allan-variance analysis follows IEEE Std 952 and El-Sheimy et al. (2008).
